units.title: The brief
units.objective: Understand what the session is really about and the three claims you need to own.

blocks.v: The session title Scale Without Sacrifice: Architecting High Volume, Always-On Payment Systems is lifted almost word-for-word from a joint Icon Solutions / MongoDB whitepaper. That paper is a benchmark: Icon's IPF running on MongoDB Atlas, pushed from 500 to 6,000 payments per second, then deliberately broken to see what happens.
If you learn one artefact in this course, make it that one. The audience will treat it as the evidence base for everything claimed on stage.
Your credibility problem, narrowed
This is not "become a payments expert". It is three specific things:

v: Domain fluency — nothing said on the panel is new to you.
Architectural depth — you can defend the benchmark against a sceptical head of payments engineering.
A point of view that is yours — the data layer as the thing that decides whether a payment platform scales, stays up, and can feed an AI.

blocks.v: Three claims to own, in your own words

v: Scale is an architecture choice, not a hardware purchase. The benchmark scaled near-linearly by adding shards and pods, not by buying a bigger box — the opposite of how most incumbent payment engines were built.

Resilience is a data-model property. Zero data loss under an ungraceful node kill came from event sourcing plus a durable journal. Recovery meant rehydrating state from persisted events, not restoring from a backup.

ISO 20022 made payments a data problem. Rich, nested, versioned, jurisdiction-variant messages are what AI and agentic use cases feed on — and are exactly what relational payment schemas handle worst.

blocks.v: Work the modules in order. Modules 1–4 buy vocabulary and arguments; modules 5–7 buy defensible depth. The architecture only lands once you know what a payment actually has to do.

units.title: The payments landscape
units.objective: Map the whole industry in one pass — instruments, schemes, business models, actors, money and rules — so that nothing later in this course arrives unexplained.

blocks.v: Every other unit in this course goes deep on one part of payments. This one goes wide. It exists because the scheme names — instant payments, faster payments, request to pay, direct debit — turn up in the resources and the conversation long before anything explains how they relate to each other, and a map you can hold in your head is worth more at this stage than depth in any single corner.

blocks.title: How to read this unit
blocks.v: This is a map, not a destination. Every area below has a module later that takes it apart properly — the anatomy of a single payment in module 01, settlement mechanics in 02, the rails market by market in 03, wallets and open banking in 04, business models in 05, regulation in 06, digital money in 07, and the technical modules from 08 to 10. Read this for orientation, then come back to it whenever a name shows up that you cannot place.

blocks.v: Two of those rows are whole layers rather than instruments, and both get a module of their own. "Wallet or overlay" covers mobile wallets and tokenisation, QR payments and offline payments, and the alias-addressed schemes — Wero, Swish, Bizum, Zelle, UPI — that sit on top of someone else's clearing. Alongside them sits open banking, which is not an instrument at all but a regulated right of access: a third party initiates a credit transfer, or reads your accounts, on a rail that already exists. Together they are the initiation layer, and module 04 takes them apart. "Digital currency" gets module 07.

The distinction that generates most of the rest is push versus pull. Push instruments put the payer in control at the moment of payment, so protection is thin afterwards. Pull instruments let the payee initiate without the payer present, so the scheme compensates with refund rights and dispute machinery. That single asymmetry explains why direct debit has an eight-week no-questions refund, why cards have chargebacks, and why instant credit transfers have neither — and therefore why authorised push payment fraud became a policy problem.

blocks.title: The uncomfortable truth to carry into every business case
blocks.v: Instant rails compress fees and destroy float. There is almost never an incremental-revenue case for instant payments infrastructure. The defensible cases are regulatory deadlines, cost-to-serve, and the ability to launch a scheme without running a programme. Saying this out loud, against your own interest, is one of the strongest credibility moves available to you.

blocks.title: The through-line
blocks.v: Every business model in this unit ends up as a non-functional requirement. A wallet that monetises float needs different data than an acquirer that monetises spread. An instant scheme's ten-second rule is a latency budget. An eight-week refund right is a retention policy. Regulation is a data requirement wearing a compliance hat. If you can walk that chain in both directions — from a commercial model down to an NFR, and back up — you can hold your own with anyone in this industry.

Where each thread continues: settlement and scheme mechanics in module 02, the rails market by market in 03, wallets, QR and open banking in 04, business models and institutions in 05, the regulatory clock in 06, stablecoins and central bank digital currencies in 07, payment hub architecture in 08, scale and data integrity in 09, and AI in 10.

Next — that is the map. The next module takes the single most important thing on it, a payment itself, and pulls it apart layer by layer. Come back here whenever a name turns up that you cannot place.

modules.subtitle: Built one layer at a time: the lifecycle, then settlement, then the vocabulary, the properties, the messages and the flows — assembled at the end

units.title: The payment lifecycle
units.objective: Narrate a payment end to end from memory, including the steps everyone forgets.

blocks.v: The four-step spine

v: Initiation — the instruction arrives from a channel: API, host-to-host file, branch, card terminal, scheme gateway.
Validation and enrichment — format, scheme rulebook, business rules, account and routing resolution, currency, calendar and cut-off logic.
Clearing — the exchange of payment instructions and the calculation of obligations between participants.
Settlement — the actual discharge of those obligations, in central bank money or commercial bank money.

blocks.v: The steps everyone forgets

v: Sanctions screening — a hard latency cost on every single payment, and a frequent source of holds.
Fraud scoring and Verification of Payee.
Limit and liquidity checks — can this customer, and can this bank, actually afford it right now?
Accounting and posting — usually the slowest and most legacy-bound integration in the platform.
Advice, reporting and reconciliation.
Exception handling — investigations, recalls, returns and repairs. Where most operational cost lives.

blocks.v: A payment is a state machine

Every payment must reach a terminal state — settled, rejected, returned. Non-terminal states (pending investigation, on hold, awaiting cover) are where risk accumulates. Hold on to this framing: everything in the architecture modules depends on seeing a payment this way.

Next — two words in that four-step spine do most of the work and are used interchangeably almost everywhere: clearing and settlement. Separating them is the next unit, because nearly everything else in payments follows from that one distinction.

units.title: Clearing is not settlement
units.objective: Distinguish RTGS from deferred net settlement, and explain how instant schemes sit between them.

blocks.v: Two settlement models

v: RTGS — real-time gross settlement. Every payment settles individually and finally in central bank money. No netting, no credit risk between participants, but high liquidity demand. T2 in the euro area, Fedwire in the US.
DNS — deferred net settlement. Obligations accumulate and net down, settling in cycles. Liquidity-efficient, but participants carry exposure to each other between cycles. ACH and CHIPS work this way.

blocks.v: Where instant payments sit

Instant schemes are a hybrid: instant and final to the customer, but underneath either prefunded (participants park cash at the clearing and settlement mechanism) or net-settled on a short cycle. This is why prefunding is a real treasury cost and a common objection in any instant-payments business case.
Push versus pull

Credit transfer, direct debit, card authorisation-then-capture, request-to-pay. Each has a different failure mode and a different dispute regime — which is exactly where card economics and account-to-account economics diverge. A card chargeback and a SEPA direct debit refund look similar to a customer and nothing alike to a bank.

The single most useful sentence you can carry out of this unit: a customer can be told a payment is confirmed before settlement has occurred, and someone is carrying risk in that gap. Know who, for each rail.

Next — you now have the mechanics of how money actually moves. What you do not yet have is precise language for which payment you are describing. The next unit supplies it: the four layers — instrument, service, scheme, rail — and why calling "instant payments" a rail is a category error.

units.title: Instrument, service, scheme, rail — what a rail actually is
units.objective: Separate the four layers that get collapsed into the word "rail", and be able to name the real rail any payment runs on.

blocks.v: You can now narrate a payment and separate clearing from settlement. This unit gives you the vocabulary to describe which payment you are talking about — and it starts by fixing a category error that is everywhere in this industry. "Instant payments", "real-time payments" and "account-to-account" are routinely called rails. None of them is one.

blocks.title: What a rail actually is
blocks.v: A rail is the concrete, named, operational path a payment travels: a clearing infrastructure, plus a settlement arrangement, speaking a defined message standard, operated by a named organisation. The test is simple — can you name the infrastructure and say where the money settles? If yes, you are describing a rail. If no, you are describing an instrument, a service, a scheme, or a property of one of them.

blocks.v: Read top to bottom: an instrument is a category, a service is a product, a scheme is a contract, and a rail is machinery. Four different kinds of thing. A sentence that mixes two of them without noticing is a sentence that will not survive a question from someone who builds this for a living.
The two facts that prove a scheme is not a rail

blocks.title: Many-to-many, in both directions
blocks.v: One scheme, two rails. SCT Inst is a single scheme with one rulebook. A euro PSP can reach it through TIPS or through RT1 — two different clearing infrastructures, with different liquidity models and different operators, carrying identical scheme rules. Same contract, different machinery. One rail, many schemes. STEP2 carries SCT, SDD Core and SDD B2B. Same machinery, three different rulebooks. If scheme and rail were the same thing, neither of these could be true.

The UK makes the split visible in the org chart. The Faster Payments scheme is owned and governed by Pay.UK. The infrastructure that actually runs it is built and operated by Vocalink — which is 97.3% owned by Mastercard. Two organisations, two layers, and one of them is a card scheme running the country's account-to-account rail. When a UK banker says "we're connecting to Faster Payments", ask whether they mean adhering to the scheme or integrating with the infrastructure. The work, the contracts and the timelines are different.
So what are instant payments, real-time payments and A2A?

blocks.title: Swift is not a rail
blocks.v: It is a messaging network. It carries instructions between institutions and settles nothing — the money moves on correspondent accounts that Swift never touches. This is the most common category error in cross-border conversations, and it matters commercially: it is why "we're on Swift" tells you nothing about how long a payment takes or who holds the liquidity. Swift gpi adds tracking to those messages. It still does not move money.

That is why "payments" as a single word is nearly meaningless, and why every serious conversation starts by pinning which layer is being discussed.

blocks.title: Four questions for a vague claim
blocks.v: When a vendor, a colleague or a press release says something imprecise about payments, ask in this order: What instrument? What service? Which scheme? Which rail? Most pitches answer two of the four confidently and slide past the others. The two they skip tell you what has not been built yet — and asking in that order, without accusation, is one of the most useful habits you can develop in this industry.

"We support instant payments" is therefore an incomplete statement, not a false one. Which scheme — SCT Inst, FedNow, RTP, Faster Payments? On which rail, where more than one exists? With what availability and what reach? Those follow-ups are not pedantry; they are the difference between an integration that takes a quarter and one that takes two years.

units.title: Topologies, processing modes and the acronym decoder
units.objective: Separate the three axes that get conflated — what sits between the endpoints, how instructions are processed, and when money becomes final — and decode the scheme acronyms without guessing.

blocks.v: The previous unit gave you one axis and one word for it: account-to-account. That word answers a question about topology — what sits between the payer and the payee. It is a real axis, but it is one of three, and most of the confusion in payments vocabulary comes from sliding between them mid-sentence. Batch, for instance, is not missing from the A2A grid because it was forgotten. It belongs to a different axis entirely.

blocks.title: Three independent axes
blocks.v: Topology — what sits between the endpoints, and who owns the relationship. Processing mode — whether instructions travel in files or one at a time. Settlement timing — when the money becomes final and who carries risk until then. They are genuinely independent: you can have any combination, and real instruments use most of them. Every time someone asks whether a payment is "real-time", ask which axis they mean.

blocks.v: Where A2A came from

Account-to-account is the oldest thing in banking wearing new clothes. European giro systems — postal giro from the early twentieth century, then bank giro — were account-to-account credit transfers by design: the payer instructs their bank to credit the payee's account, with no card, no scheme, and no intermediary owning the relationship. The SEPA Credit Transfer is that tradition standardised across a currency union.

What is new is the commercial framing. The term "account-to-account" comes from the merchant-acceptance world rather than from banking: it was coined to name an alternative to card acceptance. And it only became a real alternative when two things arrived together — open-banking APIs that let a licensed third party initiate a payment straight from the payer's bank account, and instant rails that made the money arrive fast enough for a checkout to complete. Neither the topology nor the rail was new. The combination, plus a licence to use it, was.

So when a vendor says "we do A2A", ask which of three things they mean: a PISP-initiated open-banking payment, a direct bank API integration, or a plain scheme credit transfer the merchant reconciles themselves. All three are account-to-account. Their economics, their failure modes and their reach are completely different.
Where topology is going

v: Variable Recurring Payments and commercial VRP — account-to-account with standing authority. This is the piece that has been missing: it closes the gap with direct debit and card-on-file, which is the only reason subscriptions still live on cards.
Interlinking — Project Nexus and bilateral scheme links, giving cross-border reach without anyone building a global scheme.

Tokenised deposits on a shared ledger — Swift's went into live pilot with 17 banks across six continents in July 2026. Banks keep the customer relationship while settlement moves to a shared ledger, which is a genuinely hybrid topology.
Retail central bank digital currency — the digital euro, if it ships, gives the public a direct claim on the central bank.

Agentic and delegated authority — AP2-style mandates introduce a party that is neither payer nor payee but acts for one of them. None of the topologies in the table above has a slot for that, which is exactly why the protocols are being invented rather than extended.

blocks.title: The CBDC point worth holding on to
blocks.v: Every topology in the table above ultimately routes a claim on a commercial bank. A retail CBDC routes a claim on the central bank itself. That is a change of topology, not a change of speed — and it is why the digital euro debate is about disintermediation and holding limits rather than about latency. If you only ever hear CBDC discussed as "faster payments", you are hearing it discussed wrongly.
Axis 2 — Processing mode: batch or single-message

Batch is not a speed, and it is not a generation of technology. It is a processing mode: whether instructions are accumulated into a file and handled as a group, or each one is carried end to end on its own with a response. That is independent of topology and independent of when money becomes final — which is why "batch versus real-time" and "real-time versus instant" are not the same comparison, and why batch never appeared in the account-to-account grid.

blocks.title: Batch is not legacy
blocks.v: It is the right answer whenever volume matters and latency does not — payroll, pensions, direct debits, supplier runs. Nobody wants payroll for fifty thousand employees carried as fifty thousand individual real-time messages, and no treasurer wants the intraday liquidity that would demand. The industry trend is more windows, not abolition. Treating batch as something to be eliminated is one of the fastest ways to sound naive in a payments conversation.
Axis 3 — Settlement timing

Covered properly in the next unit and in module 02, so briefly: gross settlement discharges each obligation individually and finally, usually in central bank money; net settlement accumulates obligations and offsets them in cycles, which is far cheaper in liquidity but leaves participants exposed to each other between cycles. This axis decides how much cash you must park and who is at risk while you wait.

blocks.v: Card payment is real-time at authorisation, batch at clearing and netted at settlement — so "is a card payment real-time?" has three different answers depending on which axis you mean. The promise is instant; the money is not, and that gap is precisely where chargebacks, settlement risk and working-capital cost live. UK Faster Payments is the mirror image: single-message processing but deferred net settlement. Instant to the customer, netted underneath. Instant at the service layer does not imply gross at the settlement layer.

v.def: Single Euro Payments Area — the regulatory and scheme space that makes a euro payment between member countries work like a domestic one.

Third-Party Provider, and its two flavours: Account Information Service Provider reads data on consent; Payment Initiation Service Provider initiates payments from the payer's account. PISP is the licence that makes A2A commerce possible.

Interchange Fee Regulation; Multilateral Interchange Fee; Merchant Service Charge — the EU cap, the fee it caps, and the all-in price the merchant actually pays.

SEPA's collective term for rejects, returns, refunds, reversals and revocations. Where most operational cost lives.

Open finance beyond payment accounts; auditable ICT resilience; and the EU crypto-asset regime covering stablecoin issuance, reserves and redemption.

blocks.title: Two acronym traps worth knowing before you hit them
blocks.v: OCT means two unrelated things. In a SEPA conversation it is One-Leg Out Instant Credit Transfer, an EPC scheme. In a card conversation it is Original Credit Transaction, a push to a card via Visa Direct or Mastercard Send. Context disambiguates, but only if you know both exist. CoP and VoP are not the same scheme. Confirmation of Payee is the UK's beneficiary name check; Verification of Payee is the EU's under the IPR. Same idea, different rulebooks, different match semantics and different liability. Using one name for the other in front of a European payments audience is a small tell.

This decoder covers scheme and regulatory acronyms. Module 10 carries a separate glossary of operational terms of art — cut-off, nostro, prefunding, straight-through rate, scheme pack — which is the vocabulary you use in conversation rather than the names you have to look up.

units.title: Inbound and outbound flows
units.objective: Describe both directions of a payment platform, and explain why they are not mirror images.

blocks.v: Payment platforms are almost always discussed as if there were one flow. There are two, they have different failure modes, and the difference is the single most useful thing to understand before looking at any architecture.
Outbound — you set the pace

v: Instruction arrives from a channel — API, file, branch, mobile.
Validate, enrich, resolve routing: which rail can reach this beneficiary, and what does that rail cost and require?
Risk gauntlet — sanctions, fraud, Verification of Payee, limits, duplicate detection.
Liquidity and limit check: can the customer afford it, and can the bank fund it on this rail right now?
Debit the customer, or reserve the funds.
Format to the scheme and submit.
Wait for the status message, then confirm to the customer — or unwind everything you just did.

blocks.v: The hard part is step seven. Between submission and confirmation there is a window where the outcome is genuinely unknown, and your system must model that as a state rather than an error.
Inbound — someone else started the clock

v: The scheme delivers a pacs.008. You did not choose when.
Validate, screen, resolve the beneficiary account, check its status — closed, blocked, dormant, wrong currency.
Decide: accept, reject, or accept-without-posting — within the scheme SLA.
Post the credit and make funds available.
Send the pacs.002 status back.

blocks.title: The asymmetry is the whole point
blocks.v: Outbound, you control the pace and can queue work. Inbound, a clock someone else started is already running, and under the Instant Payments Regulation you cannot decline to be reachable. That is why availability requirements bite hardest on the inbound path, and why inbound screening has to be pre-computed or extremely fast — you cannot ask the sender to wait while you think.
The flows people forget

v: On-us payments — both legs at the same institution. They never touch a scheme, so they are routinely missing from capacity models and reconciliation designs, and then someone notices that a third of volume was never counted.
Returns and R-transactions — an outbound payment that comes back is an inbound event on a payment you thought was finished.
Recalls — a camt.056 arriving about a payment you sent is an inbound request that triggers outbound work, and needs a human decision inside a scheme deadline.
Investigations — the long-tail flow with no SLA, the highest cost per item, and the worst tooling in most banks.

blocks.title: The confusion this unit exists to kill
blocks.v: Instant payments is a service. RTGS is a settlement mechanism. They are not alternatives and they are not the same kind of thing — they answer different questions and sit at different layers. An instant payment is what the customer buys; RTGS is how the resulting obligation is discharged. TIPS is a settlement service that applies the RTGS model to instant payments. modules.title: Settlement and scheme mechanics
modules.subtitle: Netting versus instant finality, pull versus prompt, and what the SLAs actually say

units.title: Net settlement versus instant schemes
units.objective: Explain why instant finality changes the liquidity model, and what that does to the architecture.

blocks.v: Deferred net settlement, and why it was invented

In a netting system, obligations accumulate over a cycle and are then offset multilaterally: if you owe me 100 and I owe you 90, only 10 moves. The liquidity saving is enormous — netting routinely reduces the funds that must actually settle by an order of magnitude — which is precisely why ACH, CHIPS and STEP2 are built this way.

The price is risk between cycles. Participants are exposed to each other until settlement completes, which is why netting systems carry net debit caps, collateral requirements and loss-sharing arrangements describing what happens if a participant fails before the cycle settles. Those arrangements are the least glamorous and most important part of the rulebook.
Instant schemes cannot net

If every payment is final the moment it is accepted, there is no cycle to net across. Each one must be backed by real funds at the moment it happens — 24 hours a day, including weekends when the RTGS system that would normally top you up is closed.

blocks.v: In a batch world the liquidity question is answered once per cycle by a treasury team. In an instant world it is answered per payment, in milliseconds, at three in the morning on a Sunday. Weekend and holiday liquidity is the practical pain nobody mentions in vendor decks: the instant rail is open, the RTGS that funds it is not, and someone has to have parked enough cash on Friday to survive until Monday without over-funding and carrying the cost.

units.title: Direct debits versus request to pay
units.objective: Understand pull payments, and why request to pay is not a payment instrument at all.

blocks.v: Direct debit is a pull

The creditor initiates, on the authority of a mandate the debtor granted earlier. Everything distinctive about direct debit follows from that inversion: the payer is not present at the moment of payment, so the scheme protects them afterwards instead.

v: SDD Core — consumers. An unconditional refund right for eight weeks, no reason required, and thirteen months for an unauthorised collection. That refund right is the product.
SDD B2B — businesses. No refund right, and in exchange the debtor's bank must verify the mandate before paying.
The mandate machinery — Unique Mandate Reference, Creditor Identifier, amendment and cancellation handling, and a pre-notification obligation before each collection.

R-transactions — rejects, refusals, returns, refunds and reversals, each with a different originator, a different deadline and a different liability outcome. This is where the operational cost of direct debit lives.

blocks.v: Request to Pay is a message, not money

SEPA Request-to-Pay (SRTP) is a messaging scheme layered above the payment rails. The payee asks the payer to pay; the payer accepts, rejects, defers or pays in part; and if they accept, a perfectly ordinary credit transfer — usually an instant one — does the actual moving. No money travels on the RtP scheme itself.

blocks.title: Why this matters strategically
blocks.v: Direct debit gives control to the creditor. Request to Pay hands control back to the payer while keeping the creditor's ability to prompt. Pair RtP with an instant credit transfer and you get billing with the creditor's certainty of being asked, the payer's control, immediate finality and no refund liability — which is why it is a structural threat to both direct debit and card-on-file billing.
Why it is architecturally awkward

An RtP is a conversation, not a transaction. It has its own lifecycle — issued, accepted, rejected, deferred, partially accepted, expired — that is separate from the lifecycle of the payment it eventually triggers, and the two must be correlated afterwards. It is a state machine sitting on top of another state machine, with a many-to-one relationship between them. Rigid schemas handle this badly, which is a point worth having ready.

The UK equivalents to know by name: Pay.UK's Request to Pay, and variable recurring payments, the open-banking mechanism that lets a payer authorise repeated variable-amount payments within limits they set — the closest thing yet to a direct debit the payer actually controls.

The originator's PSP cannot unilaterally reject once the timer is running — it must wait for a negative confirmation or the timeout. This is the rule that forces you to model "outcome unknown" properly.

blocks.v: FedNow

v: A 20-second timeout clock, configurable by the Reserve Banks.
The clock starts from the message creation timestamp, not from when FedNow receives it — so your own clock skew and internal queuing eat the budget before the network sees the message.

The receiving institution may reserve 1–5 seconds for its own response processing. If insufficient time remains for that reserved window, FedNow rejects the message immediately rather than forwarding it.
The receiver answers accept, reject, or accept without posting (ACWP) — the escape hatch for when it will honour the payment but cannot complete posting inside the window.
On timeout, FedNow rejects with a pacs.002. A resubmission needs a new message identifier, or it is rejected as a duplicate.
If no confirmation arrives, wait until 25 seconds have elapsed before sending a pacs.028 status request — sending it earlier risks creating the duplicate you are trying to avoid.

blocks.v: Both schemes make the unknown outcome a first-class case, and both defend against duplicates explicitly — new message IDs on resubmission, a mandatory wait before a status enquiry. That is a rulebook telling you to build idempotency and a status-request pattern. Take it literally; it is the same requirement the integrity unit arrives at from the engineering side.

The other practical point: ten seconds is the budget for the whole chain, not for your hop. Screening, fraud scoring, account resolution, posting, and the network itself all come out of it. Your internal share is a fraction — which is why sub-30-millisecond persistence in the benchmark is worth talking about, and why anyone quoting a database latency without stating the scheme budget it fits inside is not really making an argument.

blocks.v: The adoption gap is the story
RTP does roughly 47× FedNow's volume at about 1/26th the average ticket. That is two different use-case portfolios, not a winner and a loser.

The bigger number: the US runs at 0.12 fast payments per person per month, against 35 in Thailand, 27 in Brazil and 13 in Sweden. The honest reason is that Zelle, same-day ACH, card push payments and wallets already deliver an instant feel. There is no burning consumer need for true real-time settlement.
Cards still dominate the revenue pool

Interchange, scheme fees and acquiring. The US has no interchange cap; Europe has had one since 2015. That single regulatory difference explains most of the divergence in merchant behaviour and account-to-account adoption between the two markets — and it is the bridge into the business-models module.

units.title: Gateways, and where every acronym sits
units.objective: Place gateway, RTGS, ACH, RT1, STEP2 and TIPS on one map and never confuse them again.

blocks.v: What a payment gateway is

The term comes from card acceptance: the component that takes a payment request from a merchant's checkout, secures and tokenises the card data, and routes it to an acquirer or processor. Crucially, a gateway does not clear or settle anything. It is an access layer — connectivity, protocol translation, security and routing.

The word has since spread. Banks talk about a SWIFT gateway, a scheme gateway, a FedNow gateway. The meaning is consistent: a boundary component that fronts a network so the systems behind it do not each have to speak that network's protocol. When someone says gateway, the question to ask is which boundary.
Do not confuse it with payment orchestration, which sits a layer above and routes across multiple gateways and PSPs — choosing between them on cost, authorisation rates or availability.

blocks.v: Now the acronyms, placed

v: RTGS — both a settlement model (gross, immediate, final, in central bank money) and the systems that implement it: T2 in the euro area, Fedwire in the US. Settlement layer.
ACH — automated clearing house. Generically a batch, netted clearing system; in the US specifically the networks operating under Nacha rules, FedACH and EPN. Clearing layer.
STEP2 — EBA CLEARING's pan-European bulk CSM for SEPA credit transfers and direct debits. Europe's closest equivalent to an ACH: netted, cyclical. Clearing layer.
RT1 — EBA CLEARING's instant CSM for SCT Inst and One-Leg-Out instant transfers. Real-time gross, not netted. Clearing layer, settling in central bank funds.
TIPS — the Eurosystem's instant settlement service. It spans both layers: it clears and it settles, in central bank money, on Dedicated Cash Accounts.

blocks.title: The relationship people get wrong
blocks.v: RT1 and TIPS are often described as competitors, and for instant clearing they are. But RT1's technical account migrated into TIPS in December 2021, so RT1 settles through TIPS and a participant can manage liquidity for both in one place and exchange instant payments across them. "Competing but interconnected" is the accurate phrase, and using it correctly is a quiet credibility signal.

One more distinction worth keeping sharp: TIPS is not simply "the European FedNow". FedNow is an operator-run clearing and settlement service that institutions join directly. TIPS is a settlement service that both institutions and other clearing mechanisms connect to. The topologies differ, and so do the liquidity models.

units.title: Cross-border
units.objective: Explain correspondent banking, the G20 targets, and what is actually changing.

blocks.v: How it works today

Correspondent banking: a chain of banks holding accounts with each other. Nostro is our account with them; vostro is their account with us. A cover payment moves the funds along the chain while the instruction travels over Swift. The costs are the chain length, the trapped liquidity in nostro accounts, and the compliance check at every hop.
De-risking has shortened the chains and concentrated corridors, which is good for cost and bad for access — one of the reasons the G20 got involved.
The G20 roadmap
Four targets, and you should know all four: cost, speed, access, transparency. Swift gpi and the UETR addressed transparency and much of speed. Cost and access remain stubborn.
What is changing

v: Interlinking — connecting domestic instant systems directly rather than routing through correspondents. Project Nexus is the multilateral attempt; bilateral scheme links already exist.

Tokenised deposits — Swift's shared blockchain ledger went into live pilot on 9 July 2026 with 17 banks across six continents, moving funds continuously before final settlement through existing systems. Concept to activation in nine months.
Stablecoins — now a regulated instrument in both major markets, and therefore a genuine cross-border option rather than a crypto curiosity. Covered in the regulation module.

blocks.v: Module 01 gave you a test for a rail: can you name the infrastructure, and say where the money settles? Apply it to Apple Pay, Wero, Zelle or BLIK and the answer comes back no every time — which is the point. These are overlays. They change how a payment is addressed, who the customer thinks they are paying, and what happens when it goes wrong. They do not change the clearing. Understanding that one sentence prevents most of the category errors senior people make in this space.

blocks.title: The definition worth using
blocks.v: The World Bank's three-layer model is the cleanest formal statement: infrastructure (the clearing and settlement systems), scheme rules (procedures, standards, access, disputes), and applications — "payment services used by end users that leverage the underlying functionality of a payment system". An overlay lives in layer three. It is a product, not a rail.

blocks.v: UPI is simultaneously the overlay for banks and the rail for apps — PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm are overlays on top of it. Pix went further: Banco Central do Brasil owns the scheme and operates the settlement infrastructure, so there is no overlay operator left to capture margin. That is a design choice, not an accident, and the BIS has the evidence that it works — central-bank ownership of a fast payment system is associated with roughly 1.8% higher transaction volumes, non-bank PSP participation with 3.5%, and each additional use case with about 2%.
Europe is running two opposed strategies at once

EPI is consolidation: one scheme, one brand, built on SCT Inst, absorbing national schemes as it goes. Wero reached 43.5 million registered users and €7.5bn transferred in its first twelve months (EPI, September 2025), and 56 million users across Belgium, France and Germany by July 2026. iDEAL is being absorbed rather than co-branded indefinitely: phase two starts October 2026, full migration targets 31 December 2027, and at least fifteen million Dutch consumers move.

EuroPA is federation: Bizum, SIBS/MB WAY, Bancomat and Vipps MobilePay linked by phone-number addressing, joined by BLIK in 2025, with the first pilot euro transfer completing in December 2025. Same objective, opposite theory of change — one says replace the incumbents, the other says connect them. Which one wins is the live commercial question for 2027 and 2028, and it is a better thing to have a view on than any technology question in this module.

blocks.v: Tokenisation — what actually travels when someone taps a phone

v: The customer adds a card to a wallet. The wallet asks a Token Service Provider for a token; the issuer performs identification and verification and approves.
The wallet receives a payment token — a device-bound number, often called a DPAN — which is provisioned into a secure element or into host software.
At the point of sale the wallet presents the token plus a cryptogram unique to that transaction. The merchant and the acquirer never see the real card number.
The token travels the whole chain — terminal, acquirer, network — and the issuer or TSP maps it back to the underlying card for authorisation.
Token Domain Restriction Controls bind the token to a presentment mode, a device and sometimes a merchant, so a stolen token without its matching device and cryptogram is close to worthless.

blocks.v: The secure-element versus host-card-emulation distinction is a routing decision, not marketing. With a secure element the NFC controller routes the reader's data straight to the element and no application is involved; with HCE it routes to the host CPU and your key material lives in software plus cloud rotation. Handset-maker wallets use secure elements as standard; many third-party and bank wallets use HCE. They therefore have structurally different risk profiles, and the US Payments Forum says so plainly — software-only implementations raise malware exposure, particularly on rooted devices.

Everything else — PAR, TRID, domain controls, the wallet market structure, why handset makers ended up holding so much power — follows from that one move. And note what it did not do: the rail underneath is the same card rail it always was.

units.title: Mobile, QR and offline payments
units.objective: Know what is actually encoded in a payment QR code, why Europe went a different way from Asia, and what "offline" means in the three distinct senses people confuse.

blocks.v: Wallets, QR and offline are usually presented as three technologies. They are better understood as three answers to one question: how does an overlay reach the point of payment when there is no card terminal, or no network, or no merchant hardware at all? Each answer carries a different risk model, and that is the part worth knowing.
QR: two specifications, one payload format

head: Merchant-presented (MPM)
Consumer-presented (CPM)
rows: The merchant — sticker, screen or printed slip
None — a printed sticker is sufficient
A scanner at the till or gate
Pull-like — the merchant controls the moment
Transit gates and anywhere timing must be merchant-controlled

blocks.v: Both EMVCo QR specifications have been at version 1.1 since November 2020, with two bulletins since — merchant channel data in 2021 and merchant country-of-origin data in 2022. Stability is the point: the format stopped being the problem years ago. What is encoded is not a URL but structured data in an identifier-length-value format, flexible enough to carry several payment systems' identifiers in one code. Singapore's SGQR exploits exactly that — one code, eight payment systems, the consumer picks.
Interoperability is two independent choices, not one

v: Front-end harmonisation — everyone uses the same code format. India did this: Bharat QR and UPI QR were made interoperable and every proprietary QR code had to migrate by 31 March 2022.
Back-end connection — different systems agree APIs and settlement without touching the code format at all.

The two are delinked. You can standardise the code and leave the systems separate, or connect the systems and leave the codes different. Most national programmes do both, but they are separate decisions with separate politics.
QRIS (Indonesia) is the cleanest example of a mandated national EMVCo profile — launched August 2019, mandatory from 31 December 2019, with a per-transaction cap.
Europe went a third way, and it is the contrarian slide in this unit.

blocks.title: What Europe actually did with QR
blocks.v: EPC069-12 specifies a cleartext payload for SEPA Credit Transfer QR codes — service tag, BIC, beneficiary name, IBAN, amount, purpose, remittance information, constrained to a 331-byte payload. But for mobile-initiated credit transfers, the EPC records that the market rejected the cleartext model during public consultation and adopted a URL-based structure instead, submitted to ISO TC 68/SC 9 by fast track, with an annex mapping the payload onto EMVCo's merchant-presented format for future convergence. Europe has two QR standards and is quietly converging on the global one.
Offline: three different problems people call by one name

head: Sense of "offline"
What is missing
How it is solved today
Who carries the risk
rows: Connectivity between the merchant and the acquirer
Deferred authorisation — capture now, send when the link returns; floor limits
The merchant, until the issuer approves
EMV offline data authentication against on-card data, with card-authentication keys held at the terminal
The merchant and the acquirer, bounded by limits
Any third party at the moment of payment
Pre-funded value transferred device to device between secure elements, settled locally
Nobody can arbitrate — so exposure is capped instead

blocks.v: Open-loop transit is the best-documented offline system in production, and the constraint is physics rather than policy: a gate must give a go or no-go decision within roughly 500 milliseconds of a tap. There is simply no room for a real-time online authorisation in that budget, so the terminal performs offline data authentication locally, the cardholder verification method is necessarily no CVM, and fares are aggregated before settlement — which is why the charge on the statement never matches one journey. The residual risk is explicit: the issuer may decline after the rider has already travelled. Operators manage it with deny lists, zero-value or one-unit account status checks, and pre-authorised holds.
Offline digital money — the third case, taken seriously

v: The digital euro will have an offline mode: a proximity payment using contactless technology, directly between two devices, with an offline applet in a secure element providing secure storage, debit and credit. Critically, final settlement occurs locally — cash-like privacy, centrally issued and centrally governed.
It is pre-funded. Users load the offline balance online through their PSP, then tap phone to phone or phone to terminal. Only the payer and payee know the transaction details.

e-CNY has had dual-offline since the start, with risk managed by tiered wallets — the lowest openable with a phone number alone — and hardware wallets spanning cards, phone chips and wearables. The governing principle is stated plainly by the PBoC: anonymous for small value, traceable for high value.

The honest architectural statement, and it applies to every offline system in production: double-spend is not prevented, it is bounded. Value limits, KYC-tiered caps, deny lists, pre-funded balances and tamper-resistant secure elements cap the exposure. None of them detect a double-spend in the moment.

blocks.v: For an architect, offline is a second product, not a flag on the first one. It needs hardware attestation, a distinct reconciliation path, its own limit framework and its own dispute story. When someone proposes adding "offline support" to a roadmap, that is the pushback.
Where this is going: linking overlays across borders

v: QR linkages scale fast because they require only an agreed code format and a settlement bank, and they mostly serve inbound tourists. Thailand alone now runs QR linkages with nine jurisdictions.

A2A linkages are slower because they need scheme, legal finality, AML and FX alignment. PromptPay–PayNow (April 2021) was the first, capped at S$1,000 a day; UPI–PayNow (February 2023) is bidirectional but restricted by purpose code to family maintenance and gifts — regulators treating an overlay linkage as a remittance channel, not a general rail.
DuitNow–QRIS shows the design that makes these economic: direct local-currency quotation by appointed cross-currency dealer banks, bypassing the dollar leg entirely.

Project Nexus has crossed from research to institution. The central banks of India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand established Nexus Global Payments as a legal entity in 2025, with the BIS stepping back from operator to adviser. Connect once to a platform rather than building bilateral links; target under sixty seconds.

But the gap is still wide. Of 54 fast payment systems surveyed at the end of 2024, 37% can accept international payments, 30% can send them, and 70% use ISO 20022. Interlinking is a stated direction, not a current fact.

blocks.v: Next — QR and wallets change the interface. Open banking changes who is allowed to initiate a payment at all, and on whose data. That is the next two units.

units.title: Open banking — the initiation and consent layer
units.objective: Separate open banking from instant payments cleanly, know the three regulated roles and the interface argument that shaped a decade, and be precise about what PSD3, the PSR and FIDA actually change.

blocks.title: The distinction to make first, before anything else
blocks.v: Open banking is not a rail. It is a regulated right of access to accounts, exercised through APIs, that lets a third party read data or initiate a payment on a rail that already exists. A pay-by-bank payment in the UK settles over Faster Payments; in the euro area it settles over SEPA Instant. Conflating "A2A" with "instant payments" is the most common senior-level error in this space, and the whole module falls apart if you make it.

The second thing to hold onto is that European open banking is a by-product of a payments directive, not a data-rights law. That single fact explains almost everything downstream: the scope is payment accounts only, the commercial model was never specified because access was framed as a compliance obligation, and the ambition to go wider needed a separate instrument entirely.
The three regulated roles

head: Role
What it does
What it needs
Where the money is
rows: Reads balances and transactions with the customer's consent
Authorisation, consent, and an interface that performs
Already commercial: affordability, income verification, account verification, tenant referencing
Initiates a credit transfer from the customer's account
The same, plus an authentication journey that does not lose the customer
The contested half: A2A acceptance, bill payment, top-ups
Checks funds availability before issuing a card-based instrument
The least used of the three, by a distance

blocks.v: If you remember one commercial fact from this module: AISP is where the revenue already is and PISP is where the argument is. Any strategy discussion that only talks about pay-by-bank is discussing the half that has not yet worked.
The interface argument, and why it ran for a decade

v: The technical standards under PSD2 let a bank offer either a dedicated interface (an API) or an adapted customer interface — the customer-facing channel, opened to third parties.

A bank choosing the API route also had to build a fallback interface, unless its national regulator granted an exemption. Third parties argued fallback was the only enforcement lever against a bad API; banks argued it perpetuated screen-scraping.

Exemptions were granted widely. The practical result across most of the EU was APIs of highly variable quality and no effective remedy — precisely the failure the next generation of rules is written to fix.

Standards fragmented rather than converged: Berlin Group NextGenPSD2 (implemented by more than 75% of European banks, and since 2021 folded into the broader openFinance API Framework), STET in France and Belgium, the UK's own standard, and a long tail of national variants. That fragmentation is why aggregators exist as a business at all.
Measurement is the EU's chronic weakness. There is no EU-wide usage statistic. Counts of authorised third parties are supply-side numbers and tell you nothing about adoption.

blocks.v: What PSD3 and the PSR actually change

head: Change
What it means in practice
rows: Every account servicer must maintain at least one API. The adapted-customer-interface route disappears.
The fallback interface is abolished, and screen-scraping is prohibited outright
The decade-long argument is resolved by removing both weapons and moving enforcement to performance regulation.
Response times must match the bank's own customer channels; quarterly availability and performance statistics must be published; testing facilities are mandatory.
A consent dashboard in the customer interface, granular, with withdrawal and re-establishment within 48 hours, in language that must be neutral and free of discouraging wording.
Including duplicate strong customer authentication on a payment-initiation journey, and failing to support all available authentication procedures.
Mobile and device manufacturers must allow front-end providers to store and transfer payment data on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms.

blocks.title: Status, stated carefully — this is where people get it wrong
blocks.v: PSD3 and the PSR reached provisional political agreement on 27 November 2025 and are not yet formally adopted; entry into force is expected during 2026. The substantive provisions apply 21 months after entry into force, and mandatory Verification of Payee at 27 months — so application lands in 2028, conditional on that entry into force. FIDA is a different story: it is stalled. Trilogues opened in March 2025, the second was in June 2025, and a Commission non-paper of April 2026 exists precisely to present options for unblocking it. Any FIDA application date you see quoted is speculation.

The teaching line: Europe is about to finish rebuilding the plumbing while the ambition sits stalled. Open banking gets fixed by the PSR. Open finance — mortgages, savings, investments, pensions, insurance, credit data — does not yet exist in EU law, and the thing blocking it is not technical. It is the treatment of large platform gatekeepers, the definition of raw data, and the scope of historical data. FIDA also does something PSD2 refused to do: it builds compensation for data holders into the design. Hold that thought for the next unit, because it is the same argument the UK and the US are now having.
Consent architecture — the part that is actually yours to build

v: A consent is a durable object with a lifecycle, not a flag: granted, scoped, time-bounded, amendable, revocable, expiring, and re-establishable. Model it as such or you will retrofit it later under regulatory pressure.

Scope has to be granular and queryable — which accounts, which data categories, which period, for what stated purpose — because the dashboard has to render it and the customer has to withdraw part of it.

Authentication journeys come in three shapes: redirect, decoupled and embedded. The choice determines conversion, and conversion determines whether pay-by-bank works commercially. This is a product decision dressed as a technical one.

A payment mandate is a longer-lived consent with limits attached — an amount ceiling, a frequency, a validity period, a named payee. That is what makes variable recurring payments possible, and it is the primitive the next unit is built on.

Every consent decision is an event. Who granted it, when, through which journey, with what evidence, and what changed. The audit question is not "what is the current state" but "what was the state on the day of the disputed payment".

blocks.v: Next — the rules are one thing; what each market did with them is another. The next unit compares the UK, the EU, the US, Canada and four other markets, and answers the only question that actually decides adoption: who pays for the API.

units.title: Market by market — and who pays for the API
units.objective: Compare seven open banking regimes on like terms, and be able to argue the one question that decides whether any of them works commercially.

blocks.v: Every market answered the same three questions differently: who is compelled to open up, how wide is the scope, and who pays for the access. Those three answers predict the outcome better than anything technical. This unit walks the answers and then makes the argument that ties them together.
The United Kingdom — the only regime with real usage data

The UK's open banking originates from competition law, not PSD2: the CMA's 2017 retail banking order compelled the nine largest banks to build common APIs, funded and governed centrally. That is why the UK alone has a single standard, a single directory and published monthly statistics, and why the EU has none of those things. The CMA confirmed the roadmap complete in September 2024 — which ended the build mandate and opened the governance succession question that is still open today.

v: Sweeping VRP — me-to-me, moving surplus to savings or repaying an overdraft — was mandated on the nine banks and made fee-free to the third party. It worked technically and built no commercial ecosystem, because nobody could charge for it. It grew 98% in 2025, against 52% for single payments.

Commercial VRP — me-to-business — is the unlock, and it is the first A2A instrument that can genuinely substitute for a card on file or a direct debit: push-initiated, real-time, limits visible and revocable in the banking app, no interchange. The first live commercial VRP transaction was an energy bill in November 2025.

The UK Payments Initiative scheme, backed by 31 founding firms, launched on 2 June 2026 — the first new UK payment scheme in about two decades. Wave one deliberately targets lower-risk regulated sectors: utilities, financial services, government and charities. E-commerce comes later.

And here is the part that matters most: the per-transaction fee banks charge payment initiators is set by a pricing committee overseen by the regulators, not negotiated bilaterally. The UK has created a regulated multilateral fee for account-to-account payments — the precise thing PSD2 refused to do.

Governance is mid-transition, not settled. The FCA has designed a not-for-profit Future Entity as the standard-setting body — with no enforcement powers of its own — and expects to consult on the long-term framework before the end of 2026, with legislation giving it rule-making powers expected in 2026.

blocks.v: When the rule is unenforced, access reverts to bilateral market power. The United States has the most commercially sophisticated data-access industry in the world and it is currently being priced by whoever holds the largest deposit base. That is not an argument against open banking — it is an argument that the access question and the payment question are inseparable.

blocks.v: Two numbers in that table are not comparable and you should say so before anyone else does. Brazil's 208.8 million consents and the UK's 351 million payments measure different things. A consent is permission; a payment is use. India's 1.97 billion consents are larger still and include no payment initiation at all. Anyone putting those three on the same chart is producing a ranking of regulatory design, not of adoption. And Nigeria is not live — a go-live announced for August 2025 was missed, and as of August 2026 the framework exists without execution.
The business case, and it turns entirely on ticket size

v: European card interchange is capped at 0.2% for consumer debit and 0.3% for consumer credit. A2A's pitch is a flat fee against an ad valorem cap — which means the business case is a function of average basket size, and nothing else.

It is compelling for a £900 tax bill and marginal for a £6 coffee. HMRC's pay-by-bank took £12 billion across 3.6 million transactions in twelve months to January 2025 — an average ticket around £3,300. At that value card acceptance is economically impossible, so A2A is not displacing cards there; it is displacing bank-transfer friction.
That is exactly why the UK scheme's first wave is utilities, financial services, government and charities. It is not caution. It is arithmetic.

The regional evidence is stark: A2A is 44% of online spend in Thailand and 19% of Hong Kong e-commerce, and single-digit in most of Europe and the US. Where a mandated, free, ubiquitous real-time rail already exists — PromptPay, PayNow, UPI, Pix — A2A wins on its own. Where it has to be assembled from bank APIs plus a scheme plus a fee model, it takes a decade.

US consumer readiness is real but shallow: 85.8% of consumers have a mobile banking or payment app, but only 21.3% made a mobile point-of-sale payment in 2025. The Kansas City Fed's conclusion is worth borrowing — tap-to-pay is a more promising pay-by-bank vector in the US than scan-to-pay, because the habit already exists.

Merchant pull is no longer theoretical. Walmart is extending pay-by-bank with Fiserv, moving from multi-day ACH to instant settlement over the US instant rails, explicitly to reduce card acceptance cost.

blocks.title: The argument to make on a Sibos stage
blocks.v: Three jurisdictions answered "who pays for the API" in the same eighteen months and answered it differently. The UK regulated a multilateral access fee. The US let bilateral market power decide it. The EU kept access free under the PSR while writing compensation into FIDA. Each is now failing, or succeeding, in exactly the way its design predicts. The convergent answer emerging across all three is that the party who monetises the access pays for it — and the UK is the first serious attempt at the synthesis.
Next — that closes the initiation layer. Module 05 goes back to the money: the five revenue lines, who is licensed to do what, and which operator archetype you are actually talking to.

units.title: The five revenue lines
units.objective: Explain whose P&L a platform decision hits.

blocks.v: Technology arguments lose to economics arguments inside a bank. If you can name the P&L line, you stop being the database person and start being the industry principal.

v: Transaction fees — per-payment pricing, heavily commoditised in Europe.
Interchange and scheme fees — the card stack. Capped in the EU since 2015, uncapped in the US.
Float and net interest income — earnings on balances held between instruction and settlement.
FX spread — often the largest single margin in cross-border, and the one PSD3 forces into the open.
Value-added services — data, fraud, reconciliation, working capital, cash forecasting.

blocks.title: The uncomfortable truth about instant payments
blocks.v: Instant rails destroy float and compress transaction fees. There is almost never an incremental-revenue case for instant payments infrastructure. The defensible cases are regulatory deadlines, cost-to-serve, and the ability to launch a new scheme without running a programme. Saying this out loud, against your own interest, is one of the strongest credibility moves available to you.
Cost-to-serve is the real metric

v: Cost per transaction at peak, not at average.
Cost of a failed payment — typically an order of magnitude higher than a successful one.
Cost of an investigation, and the straight-through rate that determines how many you get.
Cost of absorbing a scheme mandate release, twice a year, forever.

blocks.v: These four are what a payments COO actually manages. They are also the bridge from architecture to economics: every one of them is a function of platform design.

units.title: Who is who, and what their licence lets them do
units.objective: Name the institution types in any payment flow and say what each is licensed and exposed to.

blocks.v: Two rules make this whole taxonomy tractable. The licence determines what you are allowed to do. The risk you bear determines what you buy. Everything below is an application of those two.
The account-holding side

v: Banks / credit institutions — take deposits, hold customer accounts, and can hold accounts at the central bank. Direct access to RTGS settlement is the deepest structural privilege in payments, and it is what everyone else is ultimately renting.

Payment institutions (PIs) — licensed under PSD2, and under PSD3 in a regime merged with e-money. They execute payments but cannot take deposits. EU policy has been steadily opening payment-system access to them, and under the Instant Payments Regulation non-bank PSPs pick up instant obligations from April 2027.
E-money institutions (EMIs) — issue electronic money against received funds. PSD3 folds them into the payment-institution regime, which is one of the package's quieter but more consequential changes.
Banking-as-a-service providers — rent their licence and rails to non-licensed brands. The regulatory question is always who is actually accountable when something fails.

blocks.v: The card side

v: Issuer — gives the cardholder the card, carries credit and fraud loss.
Acquirer — contracts with the merchant, carries merchant credit risk and chargeback exposure.
Scheme — Visa, Mastercard and the domestic schemes. Sets rules, sets interchange, moves no money itself.
Processor — does the technical work on behalf of issuers or acquirers. A large share of the industry's actual transaction processing sits here, invisibly.
Payment facilitator (PayFac) — aggregates sub-merchants under its own acquiring relationship, taking on their onboarding and fraud risk in exchange for speed and margin.
Merchant of record — the legal seller. Owns tax, compliance and chargeback liability for the sale. Distinct from who processes the payment, and routinely confused with it.

blocks.v: The open-banking side

v: AISP — account information service provider. Reads account data with the customer's consent.
PISP — payment initiation service provider. Initiates a payment directly from the customer's bank account, bypassing the card rails entirely. This is the licence that makes A2A commerce possible.
TPP — the umbrella term for both. FIDA extends the same logic beyond payment accounts into the wider product estate.

Why VoP is the interesting one

Verification of Payee checks the beneficiary name against the IBAN before the payment is sent, and returns one of three outcomes: match, close match (with the actual name disclosed), or no match. The payer then chooses whether to proceed — and if they proceed against a warning, liability shifts.
Three things this forces on a bank, and they are all data-platform capabilities:

v: A real-time queryable beneficiary directory, available 24/7 with sub-second response. A nightly batch file cannot satisfy this.
Fuzzy name matching at scale, tuned to avoid both false negatives (which annoy customers) and false positives (which defeat the purpose).
A durable audit record of what was shown to the payer and what they chose, retained for the life of any potential dispute.

units.title: Stablecoins — mechanics, reserves and the two rulebooks
units.objective: Take stablecoins apart with the same instrument / scheme / rail model you used for everything else, know where the run risk actually sits, and be precise about MiCA and the GENIUS Act.

blocks.title: Apply the model you already have
blocks.v: A stablecoin is an instrument. The chain it moves on is the rail. The issuer's terms — who may redeem, at what size, on what timetable — are the scheme rules. The wallet or exchange is the service. Nothing about this is new; what is new is that one private company can occupy all four layers at once, which no card scheme or clearing system has ever been allowed to do.
The taxonomy, and which parts matter

blocks.v: MiCA uses its own vocabulary and you should use it in Europe: an e-money token (EMT) references a single fiat currency, is e-money-like, and is redeemable at par on demand with no interest. An asset-referenced token (ART) references a basket, several currencies or a commodity. Almost every stablecoin a payments person cares about is an EMT.
The market is a duopoly, and that is a scheme-risk fact

blocks.v: Two issuers hold about 85% of the instrument. There is no multi-bank scheme here, no shared rulebook, no mutualised default arrangement. For a payments architect the implication is uncomfortable and worth stating: scheme risk and issuer risk are the same risk, and your concentration analysis has one name in it, not forty.
Reserves, attestation and where the run actually starts

v: The two market leaders sit at opposite ends of the disclosure spectrum. One publishes a quarterly attestation of its reserves report; the other publishes a monthly attestation against auditing-profession standards, holds the majority of reserves in an SEC-registered money market fund with daily holdings published by its manager, and is itself audited.
An attestation is not an audit. An attestation reports agreed figures at a point in time; an audit opines on the financial statements and the controls behind them. Know which one you are being shown.

The run risk is not in the assets — short-dated Treasury bills are about as liquid as finance gets. It is in the redemption channel. Par redemption is a contractual promise to authorised participants, typically next-day and above a minimum size. Everyone else exits into the secondary market at whatever price clears.

So the transmission is: secondary-market discount → authorised participants redeem → the issuer sells Treasury bills → a fire sale into a market that also funds the repo complex. That is the systemic channel regulators care about, and the reserve composition does not remove it.

The GENIUS Act mandates a published redemption policy. It does not mandate intraday redemption. Read every issuer's policy for the minimum size and the cut-off, because that is the number that determines your liquidity behaviour in stress.

blocks.v: The BIS critique, and the one part payments people under-rate

The BIS argued in its 2025 annual report that stablecoins fail three tests: singleness (one token from one issuer need not trade at par with another), elasticity, and integrity. The integrity argument is well rehearsed. The elasticity argument is the one that should change a payments architect's plan.

blocks.title: The constraint that actually binds B2B cross-border
blocks.v: In the BIS's words, any additional supply of stablecoins "requires full upfront payment by its holders — ie a strict cash-in-advance setup". A stablecoin cannot create intraday credit. A correspondent bank can, and routinely does, through intraday overdraft. So the binding constraint on stablecoin B2B settlement is not compliance and not volatility — it is that the instrument structurally cannot do the one thing correspondent banking does to smooth liquidity across time zones. Every serious corridor design has to answer that with pre-funding, and pre-funding is exactly the cost the corridor was meant to remove.
The two rulebooks, stated accurately

head: MiCA (EU)
GENIUS Act (US)
rows: Titles III and IV — the stablecoin titles — applied from 30 June 2024; the rest of MiCA from 30 December 2024

Not authorised — float income accrues to the issuer

The live fight is over fungible multi-issuance structures — see the note below

blocks.v: Two corrections worth carrying, because both are commonly misstated. MiCA's stablecoin titles applied six months before the rest of the regulation, not on 30 December 2024 — issuers were in scope before the exchanges listing them. And the GENIUS Act has two clocks: general effectiveness in 2027, but the prohibition on service providers offering non-compliant stablecoins bites on 18 July 2028. For exchanges and wallets, 2028 is the real cliff.

The sharpest European issue is not delisting but fungibility. The ESRB recommended in September 2025 that the Commission state that multi-issuance schemes — the same token issued partly by an EU entity and partly by a third-country entity, fungible on-chain — are not permitted, or else build a safeguards framework. The risk it names is precise: reserves fragment across jurisdictions while redemption pressure lands on the EU entity. That determines whether a global stablecoin can have an EU tranche at all, which is a bigger question than any licensing detail.
Where they are actually being used

v: Card scheme settlement. Visa's stablecoin settlement reached a $7bn annualised run rate, up 50% quarter on quarter, and added five chains in April 2026 for nine in total. Note exactly what changed: the instrument and the scheme rules are untouched. Only the settlement rail moved. That is the cleanest live demonstration of the four-layer model you will find.
B2B cross-border settlement is the largest reported use by value — the prefunded-corridor case, where the alternative is a nostro balance sitting idle.
Treasury and merchant settlement through payment platforms, mostly as a faster settlement leg rather than as the consumer-facing instrument.
Remittances get the headlines and are the hardest case: the first and last mile are still cash-in and cash-out, which is where most of the cost always was.

Be careful with volume figures. Most stablecoin "payment volume" numbers are company-reported or derived from on-chain activity that includes exchange and treasury movement. Say "reported" and give the source.

v.q: If the reserves are 1:1 in Treasury bills, where is the run risk?
v.a: In the redemption channel. Par redemption is a promise to authorised participants, at a minimum size and usually next-day; retail exits into the secondary market. A Treasury portfolio is liquid but has to be sold, and that is the fire-sale transmission.

v.q: Isn't on-chain finality better than ours?
v.a: They are different things. Probabilistic settlement finality on a chain is not legal finality under a designated-system regime. You can have irreversible bits and a reversible legal claim at the same time. Ask who bears the loss on a chain reorganisation — nobody has written it down.

v.q: Why can't an issuer just pay yield and compete with deposits?
v.a: Under the GENIUS Act it cannot pay it on the instrument, and MiCA forbids interest on e-money tokens. Yield reappears as distribution rebates and in tokenised money market funds — so model the deposit-substitution threat as coming from tokenised funds, not from payment stablecoins.

v.q: Does MiCA actually stop a US stablecoin in Europe?
v.a: Not directly. But the fungibility question would stop the EU-tranche structure that makes a global stablecoin usable in Europe, and that is the live risk to any EU stablecoin product plan.

units.title: The digital euro
units.objective: Know the legislative state precisely, understand the reverse waterfall well enough to see why it is the hardest thing on the build list, and be able to argue both sides of the disintermediation debate.

blocks.v: The digital euro is the largest single piece of new payment infrastructure Europe has committed to this decade, and for a payments architect it arrives as four things at once: a new instrument you are obliged to distribute, a new scheme rulebook, a new rail you do not control, and a real-time integration into your core banking at authorisation time. Most commentary covers the first and ignores the fourth, which is the expensive one.
Where it actually is

head: When
What happened
rows: Commission proposes the single currency package
The ECB Governing Council moves the project to its next phase, conditional on the legislation
European Parliament agrees its plenary position
Trilogues under way; the ECB's timeline assumes adoption during 2026

blocks.title: Say this carefully, because almost everyone gets it wrong
blocks.v: No holding limit has been set. The figure of €3,000 that circulates is a hypothetical used in the ECB's own financial-stability modelling, not a decision. Under the Council's position the ECB sets limits within an overall ceiling agreed by the Council, reviewed at least every two years; the Parliament's position puts the ceiling in a Commission delegated act. Legal entities may not hold a balance at all — only receive one temporarily. The Parliament made the prohibition on remuneration permanent.
The reverse waterfall is the architectural crux

A holding limit is only workable because a payment exceeding the wallet balance automatically pulls the shortfall from the user's linked commercial bank account at the moment of payment. Technically, the digital euro wallet is an overlay on an account you already service — not a standalone balance. That single mechanism is simultaneously the thing that caps disintermediation risk and the hardest item on your build list, because it demands real-time, authorisation-time access to the funding account at card-grade latency and availability. If you are planning this work, plan the reverse waterfall first; everything else is conventional scheme onboarding.
It is price-regulated from day one

v: The Eurosystem charges no scheme or processing fees. Consumers pay nothing for basic use.
Under the Council's position, for a five-year transition merchant charges are capped by reference to fees for comparable means of payment, moving to cost-based thereafter.

So the competitive threat to banks is not primarily deposit flight. It is that a zero-scheme-fee, capped-merchant-charge instrument sits permanently underneath card interchange — and it has legal tender status.
Eurosystem development cost is put at roughly €1.3bn to 2029, with about €320m a year of operating cost thereafter, funded by seigniorage as banknotes are.

For the industry, the ECB's own estimate of bank-side investment is €4.0–5.8bn in total, around €1.0–1.44bn a year over four years — about 3.4% of significant banks' annual IT upgrade budgets. Whether you accept that framing or contest it, decide deliberately: the ECB pre-empted the cost argument by quantifying it as a rounding error.

blocks.v: The supply chain is contracted, and deliberately European

Framework agreements were announced in October 2025 across five components — alias lookup, risk and fraud, app and software development kit, offline, and secure exchange of payment information — each with a first- and second-ranked provider, with work cascading to the second only if required and no payment made at signature. Core settlement, clearing and issuance go to six national central banks. Every provider is EU-controlled. Strategic autonomy is an explicit design constraint here, not rhetoric — and the fact that a banknote-security vendor won the offline component tells you what kind of problem offline is.

The industry's case

blocks.v: Notice that the two sides are not actually arguing about the same thing. The ECB is answering a balance-sheet question and the industry is asking a P&L question. The honest position is that the balance-sheet risk looks manageable and the revenue question is genuinely unresolved. Saying that in a room is more useful than picking a side.

v.q: Why would a customer use it when SEPA Instant already exists?
v.a: Legal tender status and universal acceptance, offline capability, and zero consumer cost. Against that: no interest, a holding cap, and no credit function. It is designed as a cash analogue, not a deposit analogue — judge adoption on that basis.

v.q: What if the regulation slips past 2026?
v.a: The 2029 issuance date slips with it. The ECB has explicitly conditioned its timeline on adoption during 2026 and reserved the final issuance decision until after adoption.

v.q: What is the single biggest item on our build list?
v.a: The reverse waterfall — real-time, authorisation-time access to the funding account. Not the wallet, not the app, not the scheme onboarding.
