units.title: The United States — no retail CBDC, and what replaced it
units.objective: Explain why the American answer to the digital euro is private, and distinguish a tokenised deposit from a stablecoin well enough to survive a challenge.

blocks.title: The sharpest contrast available in payments right now
blocks.v: Europe is legislating a public digital currency. The United States has prohibited its agencies from building one and is regulating private substitutes instead. Same problem, opposite answers, at the same time. If you need one slide that frames the whole of digital money in 2026, it is this one.
The prohibition, and how firm it actually is

v: Executive Order 14178, signed 23 January 2025, prohibits agencies from taking any action to establish, issue or promote a central bank digital currency, and terminates ongoing agency work immediately. It revoked the previous administration's digital-asset executive order.

It is an executive action, undoable by the next president — which is precisely why Congress keeps trying to codify it. The Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act passed the House in July 2025 and is not law.

There is still no US market-structure statute for digital assets. The CLARITY Act passed the House in July 2025, advanced out of Senate Banking in May 2026, and failed cloture 49–50 on 15 September 2026 — held up by ethics provisions, not by the market-structure substance.

So the honest position: stablecoins have a statute; everything else is being run by agency rulemaking without a statutory foundation. Plan for no US retail CBDC this decade, and treat the residual risk as an executive-branch reversal rather than a Federal Reserve initiative.

blocks.v: What is underneath instead: the instant rails, and their asymmetry

head: FedNow
RTP (The Clearing House)
rows: The rail carrying the actual retail and corporate volume

blocks.v: FedNow has roughly 45% more participating banks and about 47 times fewer transactions. Reach is not usage — many participants are receive-only, and the binding constraint on US instant payments is corporate origination and use-case demand, not network coverage. Put it against the rest of the world and the picture is stark: combined US fast-payment usage was around 0.12 transactions per person per month in early 2026, against roughly 35 for PromptPay, 27 for Pix and 11 for UPI. That consumer-side vacuum is exactly the space cards, peer-to-peer apps and now stablecoins occupy — and it is why the American answer to the digital euro is a private-instrument answer.
Tokenised deposits — a bank liability on a public chain

In November 2025 a US bank put a dollar deposit token live on a permissionless Ethereum layer-2 for institutional clients, offering near-instant round-the-clock settlement. The novelty is regulatory, not technical: a deposit liability transferable on a public network. The token mechanics are unremarkable; the permission model is the interesting part.

head: Tokenised deposit
Payment stablecoin
rows: A liability of the issuing bank, inside the prudential perimeter
A bearer claim on a segregated reserve pool
It is deposit funding — issuing it does not shrink the bank
A customer converting deposits into it does shrink the bank
At par, through existing interbank mechanisms
Secondary market price discovery plus authorised-participant redemption
Onboarded clients only — the bank's existing KYC relationship travels with it
In principle anyone with a wallet
None of the reserve-pool kind; it is a deposit
The redemption channel, as in the stablecoin unit

blocks.v: The trade is clean and worth stating as such: a tokenised deposit removes the run-on-the-reserve mechanic and gives up open access. You cannot receive one without being onboarded. Anyone who tells you tokenised deposits are "stablecoins done properly" is skipping the access question, which is the whole reason stablecoins got traction.

The consortium answer is a scheme play, not a technology play. Three of the largest US banks are building a shared tokenised-deposit network operated by The Clearing House, which they co-own, targeting the first half of 2027, framed explicitly as a defence against deposit flight to stablecoins. Putting The Clearing House at the centre means the scheme and governance layer is the existing instant-payments apparatus. The banks are keeping their scheme and swapping the rail — the exact mirror image of what Visa did in the previous unit. Once you see that pattern you will see it everywhere.
The lever the Fed actually holds

With a retail CBDC prohibited by executive order, the Federal Reserve's remaining lever is who gets to touch its balance sheet. Governor Waller proposed in October 2025 a "payment account" — a skinny master account for payments-focused institutions, with access to the Fed's rails, no interest, possible balance caps, no daylight overdraft and expedited review. In June 2026 he framed tokenisation and stablecoins as creating new channels for global dollar intermediation that operate alongside, and sometimes in conjunction with, traditional banking — complements and competitors at once, and stated as open research questions rather than policy. Access, not issuance, is the American policy instrument.

v.q: If a deposit token is just a deposit, why build anything?
v.a: Because the deposit gains round-the-clock programmable transferability and atomic settlement against tokenised assets — things the instant rails do not offer. The build is the ledger integration and the scheme rules, not the token.

v.q: Doesn't a deposit token on a public chain reintroduce the bearer problem?
v.a: No. Transferability is permissioned at the contract level; you cannot hold it without being an onboarded client. The public chain provides reachability and composability, not anonymity.

v.q: Why is FedNow so far behind RTP on volume with more banks?
v.a: Participation is enrolment, not enablement — many participants are receive-only. The constraint is origination and use cases, not reach.

blocks.v: Why they pursue it anyway — the reasons are not the ones in the press

v: The BIS surveyed emerging-market central banks and found that payment system efficiency is at the heart of their motivations, followed by financial inclusion and risk mitigation. Inclusion is second, not first.
Cash distribution cost is a real budget line in a large, geographically dispersed country, and a digital instrument attacks it directly.
Government-to-person payments are the one use case where a state can mandate adoption on the receiving side — which is why programmability has become the centre of India's programme.

Monetary sovereignty against dollarised stablecoins is the motive that has grown fastest since 2024, and it is now doing more to sustain programmes than the inclusion argument ever did. A domestic CBDC as a defence against households holding dollar tokens is a different project from a CBDC as a payment instrument.
The pipeline is real: in Sub-Saharan Africa around 75% of central banks are engaged or planning, and more than a quarter are actively preparing for a retail launch by 2028.

blocks.v: The counter-narrative, from the IMF

blocks.title: The line worth saying on a stage
blocks.v: The financial-inclusion dividend that CBDCs were supposed to deliver was delivered by fast payment systems instead — and the institution saying so is the IMF, not a crypto sceptic. Its 2025 work finds that where a public fast payment system already exists, "the space for CBDC to exert additional competitive pressure may be limited", and that interoperability with the existing system is essential to avoid fragmentation.

Set the numbers side by side and the argument makes itself: Pix at about 27 and UPI at about 11 fast-payment transactions per person per month, against sub-1% population adoption for the two longest-running launched CBDCs. But be precise about what Pix and UPI actually are, because the lesson is easy to overstate: they are fast payment systems settling in commercial bank money, with a mandated scheme and zero or near-zero merchant pricing. The instrument stayed the same. The scheme and the pricing changed. That is a governance result, not a technology result — and it is the most transferable finding in this module.

v.q: If CBDCs work so badly, why is everyone still building them?
v.a: Because the motivation central banks rank highest is payment-system efficiency and risk mitigation, not consumer adoption — and because since 2024 the sovereignty argument against dollar stablecoins has sustained programmes that the inclusion argument alone would not have.

v.q: Is e-CNY a real threat to correspondent banking?
v.a: Not yet at scale — mBridge has processed around $55bn in total, a rounding error against correspondent volumes. But it is over 95% e-CNY-settled and now run by its participant central banks outside BIS governance, which changes the political character of the rail more than its economics.

v.q: What actually killed Drex?
v.a: Privacy. Brazil could not reconcile the transparency inherent in a shared ledger with bank-secrecy obligations at acceptable cost, and said so publicly. Every wholesale tokenisation programme inherits that constraint, including the ones in the previous unit.

v.q: So should we treat Pix and UPI as the model instead?
v.a: For inclusion outcomes, yes — the per-capita evidence is overwhelming. But note what they are: fast payment systems in commercial bank money with a mandated scheme and near-zero merchant pricing. Copy the governance, not the ledger.

units.title: The canonical hub anatomy
units.objective: Whiteboard a payment platform from memory and defend every box on it.

v: Channel and adapter layer — host-to-host, API, file, scheme gateways. Normalises everything into a canonical internal model, which in practice means ISO 20022 plus extensions.
Validation and enrichment — format, scheme rulebook, business rules, account and routing resolution, currency and calendar/cut-off logic.

Risk gauntlet — sanctions screening, fraud scoring, Verification of Payee, limits, duplicate detection. Each with its own latency budget, and each capable of parking a payment in a non-terminal state.

Orchestration engine — the workflow driving the payment through those steps, per scheme and per product, with compensation paths. In IPF this is configurable flows built in IPF Studio; in Temenos and Oracle it is the payment order engine and process framework.
Liquidity and settlement — position keeping, prefunding, RTGS interaction, netting, cut-off management, cover.
Accounting and posting — usually the slowest, most contended, most legacy-bound integration in the platform.
Operations — investigations, repairs, recalls and returns, reporting, reconciliation, scheme certification.

units.title: The architectural patterns
units.objective: Discuss the benchmark's design decisions, not just its results.

v: Event sourcing. Persist the sequence of events and derive state from them. This is why the benchmark could kill a node and rehydrate in-flight payments with zero loss. Know the trade-offs too: replay cost, schema evolution, and the need for snapshots.

CQRS. Separate the write path (an event journal tuned for durable append) from the read path (an operational data store tuned for query and reporting). In the benchmark these were two separate MongoDB clusters — five shards and six shards — for exactly this reason.

Idempotency and effectively-once processing. Networks retry; money must not. Idempotency keys, deduplication windows and the outbox pattern combine to give effectively-once semantics over at-least-once delivery.

Back-pressure. A payment hub is only as fast as its slowest downstream. Back-pressured streams — IPF's connector framework does this — stop a slow core banking system from becoming a cascading failure.
Sagas and compensation. There is no distributed transaction spanning a scheme, a core and a sanctions engine. There is a saga with reversals, and the reversals are the hard part.
State machines and terminal states. Every payment must reach one. "No payment left in limbo after a node failure" is the claim you are on stage to defend.

blocks.title: The mechanism, stated properly
blocks.v: Zero data loss on an ungraceful kill did not come from a backup. Shard rebalancing redistributed in-flight transactions, and each surviving node rebuilt payment state by replaying persisted events. State was rehydrated, not restored. That distinction is the whole argument, and it is the sentence to have ready.

units.title: The canonical model, ISO 20022, and XML versus JSON
units.objective: Explain why ISO 20022 is not a canonical model, and what a good one carries.

blocks.v: Why a canonical model exists at all

A payment platform speaks many formats in and many formats out. Map each input directly to each output and you have N×M mappings to build and maintain. Introduce one internal representation that everything maps into and out of, and you have N+M. That internal representation is the canonical model, and the arithmetic is the entire justification.
The tempting mistake
"We will just use ISO 20022 as our canonical model." It is rich, it is standard, and it is already on the wire. It is also the wrong choice, for four reasons worth being able to give quickly:

v: It is a message standard, not a state model. A pacs.008 describes an instruction at a moment in time. Your platform needs lifecycle, decisions, risk scores, internal enrichment, operator actions and audit — and the message has nowhere to put any of it.

There is no single ISO 20022. Every scheme publishes its own usage guideline — CBPR+, SCT Inst, FedNow, TCH — with different mandatory fields, different code lists and different length constraints. They conflict. Picking one as canonical means the others become second-class.
It versions annually. You will support several releases at once, indefinitely.
Not everything is ISO. ISO 8583 for cards, remaining MT traffic, proprietary bank APIs, and flat files will all outlive your project.

blocks.v: What a good canonical document carries

v: Normalised common fields — the parts every payment has, whatever arrived: parties, amounts, currency, references, dates.

The original payload, verbatim. Keep what actually arrived. It is the forensic record when a dispute, a regulator or an investigation asks what was really sent — and once you have discarded it, no amount of reprocessing brings it back.
Mapping provenance — which rule, which version, which agent or which human produced each derived field. This is what makes an automated transformation auditable rather than merely convenient.
Lifecycle state and decisions — where the payment is, what was decided, by whom, and why.

blocks.title: The two problems this actually solves
blocks.v: Rich to constrained: a payment carrying structured ISO 20022 remittance data crosses onto a legacy rail that cannot hold it, and the data is silently truncated. Sparse to rich: a bandwidth-optimised ISO 8583 message from a point of sale lacks the granularity downstream ISO 20022 compliance requires. A canonical document that keeps both the original and the normalised view lets you detect the first and enrich for the second — neither of which is possible once you have flattened everything into the target format.
XML versus JSON — and the claim to stop repeating

ISO 20022 is a model, held in a central repository. XML is its classic serialisation; JSON is an officially supported alternative syntax. So "ISO 20022 means XML" is simply wrong, and correcting it gently is a nice way to demonstrate you have read the standard rather than a summary of it.

head: XML
JSON
rows: XSD schema validation, namespaces, mature and strict
JSON Schema — later to the party, now broadly sufficient
High — tag-heavy, large on the wire
Lower, and closer to how services already work
Deep in banking middleware and scheme tooling
Native to APIs, and maps directly onto a document store
On the wire, because the schemes require it
Internally, because that is what your services and storage want

blocks.v: The practical stance most modern platforms land on: XML at the boundary, document-shaped JSON inside. The mapping between them is a real cost, and it is precisely why you build the canonical model once rather than once per scheme. It is also the cleanest version of the data-platform argument — a nested, optional-heavy structure that varies by scheme and versions every year is what a document model is for. The relational alternative is a wide sparse table or a join-heavy schema, and either way each annual release becomes a migration.

The failure mode to name if someone pushes back: over-normalising. A canonical model that discards what it could not classify is worse than no canonical model, because it destroys evidence while looking tidy.

units.title: The non-functional requirements
units.objective: State payments NFRs the way a payments COO states them.

v: Availability: 24/7/365 with no maintenance window. Instant schemes removed the batch night there was to hide in. Active-active across availability zones, and increasingly across regions because of DORA.

Latency budget: the scheme gives you a total — often a handful of seconds end to end — and you decompose it across screening, fraud, orchestration, persistence and the core. The benchmark's sub-30 ms persistence at peak matters precisely because it leaves the budget to the risk checks.
Throughput profile: payments are spiky. Salary dates, tax deadlines, Black Friday, scheme go-lives. Design for peak-to-mean ratio, never for average.
RTO / RPO: for money movement, RPO must be zero. Say it that way — it reframes the entire database conversation from performance to correctness.
Elastic scale: horizontal, in units you can add without a migration. Near-linear scaling is the claim; per-shard CPU and insert rates rising proportionally is the evidence.
Data residency and sovereignty: increasingly decisive in Europe. Keeping data in-jurisdiction while running one logical platform is a differentiating capability, not a checkbox.
Observability and auditability: every state transition traceable, retained, and reconstructable years later for a regulator or a dispute.

units.title: Horizontal scale and sharding
units.objective: Explain scale-out properly, and defend a shard key choice to someone who has designed one.

blocks.v: Scale up versus scale out

Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine. It works until it doesn't: there is a largest available box, the price curve turns vicious well before that, and the whole thing remains a single failure domain. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads the data across them. The ceiling moves from "the biggest server you can buy" to "how many servers you are willing to run".

This is the difference the benchmark was built to demonstrate. Going from 500 to 6,000 payments per second was not a hardware upgrade — it was adding shards and pods, with latency staying flat until peak.
How sharding works

v: Data is partitioned across shards by a shard key. Each shard is itself a replica set, so distribution and redundancy stay separate concerns — you are not trading one for the other.
Data is divided into chunks by key range, and a balancer moves chunks between shards to keep the distribution even.

A query that includes the shard key is targeted to a single shard. A query that does not is scatter-gather across every shard. In a payment platform, lookups by UETR or end-to-end identifier must be targeted, or your read path degrades as you grow — which is the opposite of the point.

blocks.v: Choosing the shard key — the decision that decides everything

head: Property
What you want
What goes wrong
rows: Too few values caps how far you can ever split
One value takes most writes and its shard becomes the bottleneck
A monotonically increasing key sends every new write to one shard

blocks.title: The classic payments mistake
blocks.v: Payment identifiers are usually sequential, and creation timestamps always are. Shard on either and every single new payment lands on the same shard — you have bought a distributed system and kept a single write bottleneck. The fixes are a hashed shard key, or a compound key with a high-cardinality prefix. Being able to name this trap unprompted is worth more than any amount of general enthusiasm for scale-out.
Zone sharding and data residency

Zones pin key ranges to specific regions. Put a jurisdiction attribute in the shard key, map zones onto regions, and one logical cluster serves several jurisdictions without any customer's data leaving its own. This is the cleanest answer to European data-residency requirements, and it beats the usual alternative of running a separate stack per country.

State the cost honestly when you present it: a write that must cross a region boundary pays the latency. The design question is whether the payment's write path ever needs to cross one — and for most retail flows it does not.
Replica sets, and what durability means

v: A replica set is a primary plus secondaries. Writes go to the primary and replicate.

Majority write concern means an acknowledgement only comes back once a majority of members hold the write. That is what "zero RPO" means in practice — not a slogan, a setting with a measurable latency cost.
Failover is automatic — around five seconds in the benchmark, with payment processing continuing across it.
Read preference can route reporting and analytics to secondaries so they never contend with the payment write path.

blocks.v: The benchmark as a worked example

Two clusters, split by access pattern: a five-shard event journal, append-heavy, and a six-shard operational data store tuned for query — roughly 236,000 and 196,000 operations per second respectively, on M80-class shards of 32 vCPU and 128 GB. At peak the hot shard sat near 50% CPU and the storage engine's write queue stayed at zero.

That last detail is the one to quote. Aggregate throughput hides saturation; per-shard utilisation and an empty write queue are what actually demonstrate headroom. Anyone can publish a big number — showing the per-shard curve is what makes it evidence.

units.title: Integrity, consistency and idempotency
units.objective: Explain how a distributed payment system stays correct — and get idempotency exactly right.

blocks.v: Money is not like other data. A lost message in most systems is an inconvenience; here it is a payment that either happened twice or never happened, and someone has to find out which. Everything below is about making that question answerable.
Durability first

v: Majority write concern plus journaling — the write is acknowledged only once a majority of replica-set members have it durably. Survives the loss of the primary. This is the concrete meaning of RPO zero.
Majority read concern — you never read data that could still be rolled back, which matters enormously when the thing you are reading decides whether to send money.

blocks.v: Atomicity, and why the data model decides it

A single-document update is atomic. So if a payment's state lives in one document, almost every state transition needs no distributed transaction at all — the hardest problem in the system disappears by modelling. Multi-document ACID transactions are there for the cases that genuinely span documents, such as a ledger entry and a state change that must move together.

blocks.title: The design rule
blocks.v: Make the atomic unit match the business unit. A payment is one thing conceptually, so make it one thing physically. This is the strongest practical argument for a document model in payments, and it is about correctness, not convenience — which is why it lands with engineers when "flexible schema" does not.
Idempotency — four mechanisms, and one distinction
Networks retry. At-least-once delivery is all you ever get. Effectively-once processing is what you build on top of it.

v: Idempotency key. The caller supplies a key; you store it under a unique index. On a replay you return the original result instead of re-executing. The unique index does the enforcement — the database, not the application logic, which is the point.
Deduplication window on scheme identifiers. Message ID, end-to-end ID, UETR. The schemes assume you do this: FedNow rejects a resubmission that reuses a message identifier.

Monotonic sequence per aggregate in the event journal. Appending event N+1 fails if N+1 already exists, so a duplicated command physically cannot append twice. Event sourcing gives you this almost for free.

The outbox pattern. Write the state change and the outbound message in one atomic write, then publish separately. This is what prevents both "posted but never sent" and "sent but never posted" — the two most expensive bugs in payment engineering.

blocks.title: The distinction that separates people who have done this from people who have read about it
blocks.v: Idempotency is a property of the operation, not the request. Retrying "debit account X by 100 under key K" is safe. Retrying "add 100 to the balance" can never be made safe, whatever you wrap around it. Model commands with identity, not deltas.
Consistency across services

v: There is no distributed transaction spanning a scheme, a core banking system and a sanctions engine. There is a saga: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.

The compensations are the hard part, because a compensation can itself fail. Every reversal path needs the same durability and idempotency guarantees as the forward path, and it usually gets a fraction of the design attention.

Change streams let downstream processes react to a committed state change without polling and without dual writes — the trigger is the durable write itself, which removes a whole class of race condition.

blocks.v: Two things to say precisely

v: Exactly-once does not exist on the wire. Effectively-once is achievable at the endpoint. Saying it that way marks you out; saying "we guarantee exactly-once delivery" marks you out too, in the other direction.

Reconciliation is the backstop, not a fallback. Even with everything above, you reconcile against the scheme and the ledger, because the only real proof of correctness is agreement with the counterparty. Any design that treats reconciliation as an admission of failure has misunderstood the problem.

blocks.v: Notice that the rulebooks arrived at the same place from the other direction: new message identifiers on resubmission, a mandatory wait before a status enquiry, a status-request message defined in the standard. The schemes are specifying idempotency and asking you to implement it. That is a good line.

units.title: The data-platform argument
units.objective: Make the case for a document data platform without sounding like a vendor.

blocks.v: ISO 20022 messages are deeply nested, optional-field-heavy, versioned annually and varied by scheme and jurisdiction. Modelling that relationally means either a wide sparse table or a join-heavy schema — and either way, every scheme release becomes a migration.

A document model stores the message as it is, evolves without downtime, and lets the event journal and the operational data store be tuned independently. Add horizontal sharding for throughput, replica sets with majority write concern for zero-RPO durability, zone sharding for residency, and search and vector indexes in the same platform for fraud and investigation — and you have removed most of the reasons a payment platform needs four separate data stores.

blocks.title: The ordering matters
blocks.v: Lead with durability, not flexibility. Flexibility sounds like a developer convenience; zero RPO under an ungraceful node kill sounds like a control. Make flexibility your second reason, never your first.
The operational data layer pattern

The ODL consolidates payment state that would otherwise be scattered across the hub, the core, the screening engine and the case management system. It is what makes real-time investigation, natural-language querying and AI feature extraction possible — and it is the reason the AI module works at all.

blocks.title: Why the 5/6 shard split
blocks.v: The journal and the ODS have opposite access patterns. The journal is an append-heavy write path where durability dominates; the ODS is a query-and-reporting read path. The honest limitations

Single region. No core banking system in the loop. Synthetic load. Say all three before someone else does — then reframe: the value is not the headline number, it is the shape of the curve. Near-linear scaling with flat latency means capacity becomes a procurement decision rather than a re-architecture. That is the property a bank should test for in its own environment, and the benchmark tells you what to measure.

units.title: Agentic operations — straight-through processing and exceptions
units.objective: Make the concrete operational case for agents in a bank's payment estate, with numbers, and know exactly where the agent must stop.

blocks.title: Lead with this framing
blocks.v: Straight-through processing is already automated. Nobody needs an agent for the payments that work. The value sits in the small percentage that fail — and that is also where the unstructured data lives: investigation notes, correspondent free-format messages, remittance text, local market practice. Which is why exception handling is a retrieval and reasoning problem rather than a rules problem, and why it is the first place agents genuinely earn their keep.
The problem, sized — and these are the numbers to have ready

v.s: Swift — the majority of STP failure is a data problem, not a payments problem

blocks.v: Swift's own modelled prize is about $602m a year: roughly $332m operational and $270m liquidity. The liquidity component is nearly half and is almost always left out of business cases. An unresolved investigation is not only a cost centre — it is stranded value-dated cash. And there is a revenue tail: more than 3% customer attrition is attributed to poor exceptions and investigations experience, which converts an operations argument into a CFO argument.
Why now: two hard dates inside the next fifteen months

head: Date
What changes
What it does to your queue
rows: Town name and country must appear in designated fields for all agents and parties in cross-border ISO 20022 messages. Fully unstructured addresses may be rejected or delayed — hybrid remains permitted
About 65% of messages still carried unstructured addresses in March 2026. This is a forecastable exception wave on a known date

blocks.v: There is a direct, causal chain between those two rows. The European rulebook already updated its return reason codes to cover invalid or unsupported address formats. So the address mandate will manifest as a measurable spike in a specific, known reason code. A forecastable exception wave with a known taxonomy is the cleanest pilot an operations team will ever be handed.
Where a model beats a rule — and where it does not

blocks.title: The most useful fact in this unit
blocks.v: Swift's own address-structuring tool is a conditional random field, not a large language model — open-sourced in November 2025, self-hosted, extracting town and country only, and explicitly documented as performing poorly on Arabic, Chinese, Cyrillic and Japanese. The industry's own reference tool defines exactly where the deterministic approach stops. The language model's marginal value is precisely that residual: transliteration, non-Latin script, entity resolution against reference data, and the messy long tail the deterministic model flags as low-confidence.

head: Task
Rules engine
Agent
Verdict
rows: Non-Latin script, transliteration, messy free text
Agent, with the reference data as the constraint
Classification over a closed, auditable label set
The best first production use case in the estate

blocks.v: Purpose-code inference deserves the top of your roadmap and almost nobody puts it there. Purpose codes are jurisdiction-specific, frequently mandatory for regulatory reporting, and routinely absent or wrong. Inferring one from free-text remittance information is a classification problem over a closed label set — which means it can be confidence-scored, constrained to a whitelist, and back-tested against realised rejects. That combination is rare, and it is what makes a use case provable rather than merely plausible.
The architectural rule, and the reason for it

The agent proposes with a confidence score; a deterministic validator approves. The reason is not squeamishness — it is that the failure modes are asymmetric. A rules engine fails loudly on input it does not recognise. A language model fails silently and plausibly, inventing a well-formed town name that does not exist. You want the non-deterministic component to have high recall and the deterministic component to hold the veto.

Corollary, and it is the one that makes the whole thing auditable: never let the agent's output be the only artefact. The proposal, the confidence score, the evidence retrieved and the validator's verdict all become events. That is what lets you replay six months of repairs when a supervisor asks whether a model was systematically mangling one corridor.
The exception taxonomy, and the agentic workflow over it

head: Exception class
What the agent may do
What stays human
rows: Classify, identify cause, propose repair and resubmission
Approving a resubmission that moves customer money
Gather evidence across systems, draft the enquiry, propose a disposition
Sending the enquiry, if policy requires
Assemble the evidence pack and summarise prior dispositions of similar alerts
Match candidates, explain the difference, propose the entry

blocks.v: The boundary is not a policy preference; it is architecture. The distinction that matters operationally is read versus write, enforced at the tool boundary, not in the prompt. An agent with no write tool cannot release a sanctions hit however it is instructed. An agent that has one can, and no amount of prompt engineering fixes that.

One honest caveat to carry, because it will be tested: none of this removes the human from a payment that has already failed a regulatory check. Agents compress investigation time and improve first-time-right rates. Claiming more than that in a Sibos room will cost you more than the claim is worth. And be careful with the commonly quoted "95% of sanctions alerts are false positives" — no supervisor or standard-setter publishes that figure; it traces to vendor material. What is published is Europol's finding that on average about 10% of suspicious transaction reports are further investigated and roughly 1% of criminal proceeds are confiscated. The smaller, sourced number is the stronger one to use.
Next — repair and investigation fix payments that have already gone wrong. The next unit is the harder problem: choosing better before you send, and managing the money that sits still.

units.objective: Make the case for agents that choose rather than repair: least-cost routing for remittances, and sweeping, pooling and FX for corporate treasury.

blocks.v: The previous unit fixed payments that failed. This one is about deciding better in advance — and it is where the agentic argument gets genuinely interesting, because the decisions are constrained optimisations over quantities nobody currently measures.
Remittance cost: the baseline, and where it actually comes from

v.c: global average cost of sending $200
v.s: World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide, Q3 2025 — the latest published

v.c: Sub-Saharan Africa, the most expensive region
average cost through a bank

blocks.title: The number that reframes the whole unit
blocks.v: The provider spread is far wider than the regional spread. A bank averages roughly 4.2 times the cost of a digital-only operator on the same $200. So the remittance cost problem is not fundamentally geography — it is channel and operating model. And operating model is exactly what an agent changes.

Be precise about the G20 targets, because getting them wrong is the kind of error a head of payments will catch. Retail cross-border: ≤1% global average and no corridor above 3%, by end-2027. Remittances: ≤3% average and no corridor above 5%, by 2030. Speed: 75% within one hour across all segments by end-2027. The FSB's own 2025 scorecard shows retail at 35.4% within one hour and — notably — the share settling within one business day went backwards. Its verdict on its own programme is that the KPIs show only slight improvement since 2023 and that policy milestones have not translated into tangible improvements for end users. Use that. The roadmap's own scorekeeper says the roadmap is not working, which is the argument for changing the execution layer rather than the standards.
Least-cost routing is an optimisation over predicted, not known, quantities

Known at decision time?
Why it resists a classical routing engine

Deducted downstream and discovered after the fact

blocks.title: The formulation to put on a slide
blocks.v: Expected cost of a route = quoted cost + P(repair) × cost of repair + P(investigation) × cost of investigation + liquidity cost of delay. The previous unit supplies the last three terms. Routing, repair and investigations are not three problems — they are one objective function, and almost no bank computes it, because the data lives in three systems owned by three managers. That is a data-platform argument before it is an AI argument.

A credibility point worth making out loud: the freshest published remittance cost data available today is from Q3 2025, and the latest official KPI set from October 2025. The industry is steering a 2027 target using data roughly a year stale. An operation that can compute its own realised corridor costs weekly has a decision advantage over the published benchmark — and computing that is not an AI problem at all.
Corporate liquidity: the structures, stated precisely

What it does
Constraint to know
rows: Full sweep of a participant account to a header account, daily. Cash actually moves, creating intercompany loans
Intercompany loan documentation, transfer pricing, and withholding tax in some jurisdictions
The same, but to a set floor or target rather than nil
Requires a forecast to set the target sensibly — which is the agentic opening

A treasury entity operating internal accounts for group companies

blocks.title: Why notional pooling got expensive — quote the rule, not the vibe
blocks.v: The Basel leverage ratio text is unambiguous: banks must not take account of collateral, guarantees or other credit risk mitigation to reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure, nor may they net assets and liabilities. A notional pool nets to zero economically, but the gross debit balances stay in the exposure measure — so the bank funds leverage capital against a position with no net exposure. Physical concentration does compress the balance sheet, because the cash moves and the debit is extinguished. That is the mechanism, and it is why the market shifted to sweeping and in-house banks.

One correction to the standard narrative. China is now materially more permissive than most decks assume: the integrated local- and foreign-currency cash pooling pilot was expanded to ten regions in December 2024, permitting cross-currency lending among onshore participants for current-account cross-border payments, with streamlined filing and self-determined external-debt ratios on macroprudential principles. Anyone still saying "you cannot sweep out of China" is working from pre-2024 knowledge. Do not generalise from China to other restricted markets, though — each has its own regime.
Where the agent earns its place in treasury

v: Forecast per currency and per entity. Fragmented balances cost twice: you pay bid-offer on conversions you could have netted away, and you hold buffers sized to the sum of local volatility rather than the net.

Decide sweep amounts and timings against cut-offs and value dates. Sweeping reduces both the number and the size of conversions — and the number usually matters more, because per-ticket spread on small conversions is where the cost hides.

Choose between converting, swapping and running an overdraft. This is the single best-defined agentic task in treasury: three fully quotable prices, a forecast cash profile, a value date and a cut-off. It is bounded, it has a right answer, and the answer is checkable after the fact.
Pre-position liquidity ahead of known outflows — the tax payment, the payroll run, the coupon date — instead of funding them at the wrong hour in the wrong currency.

And the control statement, which is the same one as the previous unit: treasury policy limits are a hard constraint evaluated outside the model, and execution is deterministic. An agent that can propose a sweep but cannot initiate one has a bounded blast radius. An agent with payment-initiation rights has an unbounded one.

v.q: Why would I trust a model to choose a route when I can just pick the cheapest quote?
v.a: Because the quote is the only term you can see, and it is not the term that dominates the variance. Lifting fees, cut-off misses, repair probability and the liquidity cost of delay are all larger and all learnable from your own history.

v.q: Isn't cash forecasting a solved problem?
v.a: Forecasting per entity per currency at a daily horizon with cut-off awareness is not solved at most corporates — and the evidence is that they hold buffers sized to gross rather than net exposure. That gap is the value.

v.q: What stops it from sweeping money to the wrong place?
v.a: It cannot sweep. It proposes an amount, a timing and a destination; policy limits are checked outside the model; execution is a deterministic, idempotent instruction issued by the treasury system. The agent never holds the payment-initiation tool.

units.objective: Make the architecture argument that all three preceding units depend on — and be ready for the governance and regulatory questions before anyone asks them.

blocks.title: Borrow the IMF's layering, not your own
blocks.v: The IMF's 2026 work on agentic payments uses a three-layer framework — intent, authorisation, settlement — and identifies the central tension as the incompatibility between probabilistic AI behaviour and deterministic payment infrastructure requirements. Its conclusion is worth quoting: outcomes will depend on institutional design and governance as much as on technology. Intent, authorisation and settlement map exactly onto propose, approve, execute. Use the IMF's framing rather than inventing one — it is independently authoritative and it survives a challenge.
Four agent patterns worth naming

head: Pattern
What the agent does
What it needs underneath
rows: Flags fields at risk of truncation, enriches sparse messages from internal profiles, transforms semi-structured data into ISO 20022
The original payload preserved, plus similar past exceptions retrievable by meaning
Embeds unstructured case notes and finds conceptually related past cases rather than keyword matches
Vector search over operational text, alongside the payment data
Compares true corridor cost — fees, FX spread, predicted repair and delay — against policy and recommends a settlement path
Live telemetry captured as time series, and policy the agent can read
Proposes field mappings between standards for a human to approve
Mapping provenance, so every proposal is auditable

blocks.v: The control model — seven properties, and one that surprises people

v: Typed tools. The agent acts only through declared, schema-validated tools — never free-form access to a system.
Idempotent tools. This is the one people miss. An agent that retries is normal behaviour, and in payments a retry that is not idempotent is a duplicate payment.
Read and write separated at the tool boundary, not in the prompt. An agent without a write tool cannot be talked into using one.
The agent never writes to the ledger. It writes proposals, to a path that is physically distinct from the system of record.
Every proposed action becomes an event carrying a correlation id, alongside the evidence it retrieved and the reasoning that produced it.
An approval workflow keyed on that correlation id, so the proposal, the disposition and the executed instruction are one traceable chain.
Kill switches at the tool level, not the model level. You disable capability, not intelligence — because the model can be swapped and the capability is what carries risk.

blocks.v: What the data layer has to provide

The requirement comes from the workflow, not from the model. An investigation agent needs the payment's current state and its history and the applicable policy and comparable past cases, within one reasoning turn. Today those are four systems with four latencies, and that is the actual reason agentic pilots stall.

v: A canonical document holding the native payload and the normalised fields together — the foundation from the architecture module, now doing work.
Vector search over investigation notes and past exceptions, so retrieval is by conceptual similarity rather than string matching.
Multi-document ACID transactions, because an agent-driven update to a ledger entry and a payment state must move together or not at all.
Change streams and stream processing to trigger workflows the moment state changes, without polling and without dual writes.
Global clusters and zone sharding for corridor latency and data residency.
CQRS to keep the agent's read traffic off the payment write path — the referenced payment data store sustains roughly 10,000 writes per second behind 1,000 payments per second.
A proposal store that is not the system of record, which is what makes "the agent never touches the ledger" an architectural fact rather than a promise.

blocks.v: Governance is the part that sells it

Every AI input and output logged and linked to an approval; mapping provenance recorded so any transformation can be traced to the rule, agent or human that produced it; schema validation and encryption enforcing policy. Human-in-the-loop is a design requirement here, not a disclaimer — and the audience you will be speaking to cares far more about that than about model capability.

The strategic frame is worth borrowing: this is a control-preserving alternative to rip-and-replace. A bank does not have to replace its core to get here; it has to stop throwing away the data its core cannot hold. That argument works in a room full of people who have been told to modernise and have no appetite for another five-year programme.
Which rulebook actually governs this — and the answer is not the one everyone names

blocks.title: Payment-operations AI is, in the ordinary case, not high-risk under the EU AI Act
blocks.v: The high-risk annex captures creditworthiness and credit scoring of natural persons — explicitly excepting fraud detection — and life and health insurance pricing. STP repair, exception handling, reconciliation and treasury optimisation are not enumerated. Two implications: the compliance burden people fear is largely misattributed; and an agent that starts inferring things about natural persons' creditworthiness has crossed a regulatory boundary that the same agent doing repair had not.

head: Regime
Status to state
What it actually requires of you
rows: In force since August 2024; general-purpose model obligations, governance and penalties from August 2025; general application August 2026. The Digital Omnibus adopted in June 2026 deferred high-risk obligations to December 2027 and embedded high-risk to August 2028
For most payment-operations AI: transparency and literacy obligations, not the high-risk regime
ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party and critical-provider oversight. This is the regime that actually governs your agent today
The US supervisory guidance predates machine learning entirely and does not address it explicitly
The live ambiguity is whether a non-deterministic agent producing a recommendation is a model at all. Most banks are resolving it conservatively by treating it as one
The EBA found no significant contradictions between the AI Act and EU banking and payment legislation, describing the Act as complementary
You are already regulated — just not primarily by the regulation everyone is talking about

blocks.v: Supervisory expectation is already explicit. The ECB has said that more than 85% of large supervised banks already use AI in some form, and requires "clear and unambiguous accountability for AI-driven decisions", flagging concentration risk, vendor lock-in, operational resilience and exit strategies — and insisting AI be governed as a core business and risk topic, not a technology side project. The closing line is worth carrying: information does not automatically translate into judgement.

If every proposal, its evidence and its disposition carry a correlation id, you can measure the value; if they do not, you cannot, and no additional model will fix it.

Two honest gaps to admit before someone else finds them. There is no verifiable named-bank deployment of agentic AI in payment operations in the public domain — everything out there is vendor material or trade commentary. And no standard-setter has published a reference architecture for it; the BIS, CPMI, FSB, EBA and ECB have published on risks and governance, not on design. Both absences are useful on a stage: the field is pre-reference-architecture, which is exactly why the architecture argument is worth making rather than merely quoting.

units.title: The questions that will test you
units.objective: Rehearse delivery, not content. Answers that open with a concession land better in this room.

blocks.v: Practise these out loud. Every one opens by conceding something true — that is what makes the rest credible.

v.q: "6,000 TPS is a synthetic benchmark. What does that have to do with my bank?"
v.a: Concede first: controlled benchmark, single region, twelve processing steps, no core banking system in the loop. Then reframe — the value is not the headline number, it is the shape of the curve. Near-linear scaling from 500 to 6,000 with flat latency means capacity is a procurement decision, not a re-architecture. That is the property a bank should test for in its own environment, and the benchmark tells you what to measure.

v.q: "Why would I put payments on a document database?"
v.a: Because ISO 20022 is a nested, optional-heavy, annually versioned document format, and because the write path and read path in a payment hub want opposite things. Then the durability point, which is the one that matters: replica sets with majority write concern give you zero RPO, and the ungraceful-kill test is the evidence. Do not lead with flexibility — lead with durability, and let flexibility be the second reason.

v.q: "Our bottleneck is the core banking system, not the payment engine."
v.a: Agree immediately and completely. This is true at almost every bank, and saying so buys more credibility than any statistic. Then the architectural answer: back-pressured streams so the hub degrades gracefully rather than cascading, an operational data store that absorbs read load the core would otherwise carry, and event sourcing so posting can be asynchronous without losing the audit trail. The hub's job is to stop being the constraint and to stop the core from becoming a single point of failure.

v.q: "Isn't this just a vendor pitch?"
v.a: Answer with the thing you would tell a bank not to do. For example: replacing a payment engine to chase instant-payments revenue is usually a bad business case in Europe, and the defensible cases are cost-to-serve, regulatory deadlines and the ability to launch a scheme without a programme. Specific, slightly against interest, and instantly disarming.

v.q: "How do you handle data residency across a multi-region deployment?"
v.a: Zone sharding: the shard key includes a jurisdiction attribute, zones pin ranges to regions, and one logical cluster serves multiple jurisdictions without data leaving them. Then the honest caveat — cross-region writes cost latency, so the design question is whether the payment's write path ever needs to cross a boundary, and usually it does not. Naming the cost is what makes the answer credible.

v.q: "What does agentic AI actually change for a payment service provider?"
v.a: Two things, concretely. First, authorisation stops being a single moment and becomes a mandate with constraints that must be stored, checked and revoked — infrastructure most PSPs do not have. Second, transaction volumes decouple from human attention, which breaks the assumptions behind both fraud models and capacity planning. Then be honest that the standards are unsettled and most of the industry is at pilot stage.

v.q: "Everyone claims linear scaling. Why should I believe this one?"
v.a: Because the evidence is per-shard, not aggregate. CPU and insert rates rose proportionally per shard across the ladder, the WiredTiger write queue stayed at zero, and there was roughly 40–50% headroom at the top of the range. Aggregate throughput numbers hide saturation; per-shard utilisation does not. Then invite the test: run the same ladder on their own topology.

units.title: Your ninety seconds
units.objective: Draft and rehearse the one uninterrupted stretch you will get.

blocks.v: Whatever the panel format, you get one uninterrupted stretch. This is the shape it should take. Write it in your own words and say it aloud until it stops sounding written.

v.v: The sacrifice. For twenty years, payment platforms traded one thing for another — throughput for resilience, resilience for agility, agility for control. Name the trade the audience actually lives with.

Why the trade is now unaffordable. Instant schemes removed the batch window. The IPR made 24/7 a legal obligation. DORA made recovery auditable. ISO 20022 multiplied the data. None of these are choices.
The evidence. Six thousand payments a second, half a second end to end, node killed under live load, ninety seconds to recover, zero payments lost. Scale-out, not scale-up.

The mechanism. Event sourcing and CQRS over a distributed, sharded data layer. State is rehydrated from persisted events, not restored from backup. That single design decision is what makes "zero loss" a property rather than a promise.

The consequence. The same data foundation that survives failure is the one that feeds fraud models, investigations, and next, agent mandates. You do not get an AI strategy in payments without solving the data layer first.
Hand back with a question for the panel rather than a summary. It signals confidence and keeps you in the conversation.

v.def: Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference — the UUID that makes a cross-border payment trackable across every intermediary.
The interbank customer credit transfer. The workhorse message; know its structure.
Request to cancel a payment. The opening move of most investigations.
SEPA's collective term for rejects, returns, refunds, reversals and revocations. Where most operational cost lives.
Real-time gross settlement versus deferred net settlement — individual finality versus netted cycles.
Clearing and Settlement Mechanism. TIPS and RT1 are competing CSMs for euro instant payments.
SEPA scheme variant for payments where one leg sits outside the EEA.
Verification of Payee — the IBAN/name check mandated by the IPR since October 2025.
The scheme or correspondent deadline after which a payment moves to the next value date. Instant rails removed it; everything else still runs on it.
Our account with them / their account with us. The plumbing of correspondent banking.
Cash parked at the CSM so instant payments can settle outside RTGS hours. A real treasury cost, and a common objection.
A pluggable module implementing one scheme's rulebook, messages and certification. IPF's unit of extensibility.
Operational data store or layer — the read-optimised projection of payment state. The read half of CQRS.
US corporate control where issued payment files are matched before release. Comes up in US fraud conversations.
Percentage of payments needing no human touch. The most quoted operational KPI in the industry.
In AP2, the verifiable credential recording what a user authorised an agent to do. The new unit of consent.
The funds movement that accompanies a payment instruction along the correspondent chain.
MongoDB's storage-engine write backlog. Zero under load is the evidence that persistence is not the bottleneck.
